paper_title: Neurocognitive endophenotypes in CGG KI and Fmr1 KO mouse models of Fragile X-Associated disorders: an analysis of the state of the field
paper_abstract: It has become increasingly important that the field of behavioral genetics identifies not only the gross behavioral phenotypes associated with a given mutation, but also the behavioral endophenotypes that scale with the dosage of the particular mutation being studied. Over the past few years, studies evaluating the effects of the polymorphic CGG trinucleotide repeat on the FMR1 gene underlying Fragile X-Associated Disorders have reported preliminary evidence for a behavioral endophenotype in human Fragile X Premutation carrier populations as well as the CGG knock-in (KI) mouse model. More recently, the behavioral experiments used to test the CGG KI mouse model have been extended to the Fmr1 knock-out (KO) mouse model. When combined, these data provide compelling evidence for a clear neurocognitive endophenotype in the mouse models of Fragile X-Associated Disorders such that behavioral deficits scale predictably with genetic dosage. Similarly, it appears that the CGG KI mouse effectively models the histopathology in Fragile X-Associated Disorders across CGG repeats well into the full mutation range, resulting in a reliable histopathological endophenotype. These endophenotypes may influence future research directions into treatment strategies for not only Fragile X Syndrome, but also the Fragile X Premutation and Fragile X-Associated Tremor/Ataxia Syndrome (FXTAS).
review_content:
This review by Michael Hunsaker covers a large body of literature to which he has significantly contributed related to behavioral assay development in Fragile X spectrum disorder mouse models. The author includes data from several different published reports to analyze and compare behavioral results in CGG KI premutation model mice to similar tests done in Fmr1 KO animals. Interestingly, some though not all of these data follow a trajectory related to CGG repeat length. The author goes on to comment on data comparing inclusion formation in human and mouse models, and address differences between male and female premutation patients and models. It also addresses shortcomings in the current mouse models of Fragile X spectrum disorders. The central conclusion of the paper is that the field needs to work towards development of more patient-applicable endophenotypes to allow for successful translation of basic research discoveries to successful therapeutic development.

Overall, the article is well written and the title and abstract are appropriate.

Below are a few comments that if addressed would enhance this review and make it more appropriate for indexing.
 1. Battery development and implementation: Spatial processing and Figure 1. More explanation of these behavioral tasks would aid reader comprehension. Figure 1 was included to help explain how these tests are performed, but as data are included in the review, it would be useful to have more details on methodology in either the figure legends or in the body of the text.
 2. Figures 2-5. A legend explaining that red corresponds to WT, green low CGG, and orange high CGG on these figures should be included either in the figure itself, or in the figure legend. Additionally, it was not clear that the points outside the box plot were outliers and not indicators of significance. More information about how the data are presented would be helpful. It’s also unclear why the individual data points for the WT results are not always included below the box plots. Additionally, were any statistics done on these data? An R2 value for the correlation lines, or an ANOVA for CGG repeat length, or age, would all be appropriate tests to include in these results without having to refer back to the original research manuscripts.
 3. Female premutation model mice and Figures 3 and 4: The fact that female CGG KI model mice also show differences in temporal processing with these tests is an interesting observation. Female premutation patients often show less severe symptoms when they have one copy of FMR1 with smaller repeats, making them heterozygous for the pathogenic repeat allele, owing to X-inactivation and mosaic expression. The genotype of the female mice tested in Figures 3, 4, and the text on temporal processing is not indicated, and should be included for clarity. Sex differences and X-inactivation are also mentioned with the histopathological endophenotype discussion, and warrant more explanation for those unfamiliar with the process and impact that X-inactivation skewing can have on this disorder. Additionally, the result in female mice on temporal processing begs the question if female CGG KI mice have been tested in any of the other behavioral tasks discussed in this manuscript.
 4. Figure 5: The author mentions that the Fmr1 KO mice is not a perfect model of FXS as Fmr1 expression was eliminated by inserting a neomycin cassette, and not by way of repeat expansion followed by promoter and 5’UTR hypermethylation as in the human disorder. As such, it is probably incorrect to plot the Fmr1 KO data at/beyond the 200 CGG repeat mark. These animals do not have any repeats and as such should be plotted on a separate scale.
 5. Analytical verification and Figure 7: Do the two misclassifications noted in Figure 7 correspond to obvious outlier animals? It might be interesting to look back at the data from those animals which the algorithm did not classify with the rest, and comment on why they may have been missed in the analysis.
 6. Histopathological endophenotype: The author does a nice job of accumulating histological findings in premutation patients and mouse models. However, the discussion of current hypotheses around the development of inclusion formation and disease pathogenesis is lacking. There are many theories in the FXTAS field that the increase of FMR1 mRNA can cause protein sequestration, and may also trigger production of aberrant protein products which could contribute to inclusion formation. The mechanistic data for both of these hypotheses should be at least mentioned here.
 7. Table 1: The percentages reported for frontal cortex and hippocampus are not explained – is this the percentage of inclusions in neuronal/glial cells? Additionally, inclusion of CGG repeat lengths where available should be included in this figure, as the author is commenting on the correlation of repeat length and inclusion formation.
 8. Conclusions, Behavioral endophenotype: The comment on associations between CGG length, FMR1 mRNA, and FMRP expression warrants more discussion. Illustrating in some way the differential effects of CGG repeat levels on FMR1 mRNA levels, in contrast to the decrease in FMRP expression with increasing CGG repeats would be helpful (akin to the table generated by (Brouwer et al, 2008). Further, in discussing these endophenotypes in the context of FXS and the Fmr1 KO mouse, there is a difference between no FMRP expression, reduced FMRP expression, and the toxic mRNA gain of function that are all contributing to the unique phenotypes seen in the fragile X spectrum disorders (Ludwig et al., 2014; Pretto et al., 2014)
 9. Future directions: The call for more rigorous tests to compare mouse models and human patient phenotypes is indeed warranted. However, in discussing the limitations of the current models, it should be noted that FXTAS and FXS are not unique in the failings of animal models in general. The inability of mice to completely recapitulate human neurological disease is very common, especially in neurodegenerative disease (Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease models are both notorious for lacking complete recapitulation of clinical phenotypes). All models (including human iPS cells and simple systems like worms and flies) are fraught with limitations, but there is power in multi-model analysis that one might hope would lead to a greater likelihood for translation from basic science findings to clinical practice. However, leaving the discussion on therapeutic development as disappointing solely because basic research in mouse models has not yet led to successful clinical trials in patients undermines the significant progress made in the field over the past decade.
paper_title_zh: 脆性X相关障碍的CGG KI和Fmr1 KO小鼠模型中的神经认知内表型：领域现状分析
paper_abstract_zh: 行为遗传学领域越来越需要识别的不仅是与特定突变相关的大体行为表型，还包括与所研究突变剂量成比例的行为内表型。在过去几年中，评估多态性CGG三核苷酸重复对脆性X相关障碍中FMR1基因影响的研究报告了初步证据，表明在人类脆性X前突变携带者群体以及CGG敲入（KI）小鼠模型中存在行为内表型。最近，用于测试CGG KI小鼠模型的行为实验已扩展到Fmr1敲除（KO）小鼠模型。综合这些数据，为脆性X相关障碍小鼠模型中存在明确的神经认知内表型提供了有力证据，即行为缺陷与基因剂量成可预测的比例。同样，CGG KI小鼠似乎有效地模拟了脆性X相关障碍中跨越CGG重复直至完全突变范围的病理组织学，从而形成了一个可靠的病理组织学内表型。这些内表型可能会影响未来研究治疗策略的方向，不仅针对脆性X综合征，还包括脆性X前突变和脆性X相关震颤/共济失调综合征（FXTAS）。
review_content_zh:
**评论内容翻译：**

迈克尔·亨萨克的这篇综述涵盖了大量文献，这些文献主要涉及脆性X谱系障碍小鼠模型中的行为检测开发，而他本人对此领域有显著贡献。作者综合了多篇已发表报告的数据，分析和比较了CGG KI前突变模型小鼠与Fmr1 KO动物在类似测试中的行为结果。有趣的是，尽管并非所有数据都遵循这一趋势，但部分数据显示出与CGG重复长度的相关性。作者进一步评论了人类和小鼠模型中包涵体形成的比较数据，并探讨了前突变患者和模型中男性和女性之间的差异。此外，文章还指出了当前脆性X谱系障碍小鼠模型的不足之处。论文的核心结论是，该领域需要努力开发更适用于患者的内表型，以便将基础研究发现的成果成功转化为有效的治疗方法。

总体而言，文章写得很好，标题和摘要也恰当。

以下是一些建议，若加以改进，将提升这篇综述的质量，并使其更适合索引：
1. **电池开发与实施：空间处理和图1**。对这些行为任务的更多解释将有助于读者理解。图1的目的是帮助解释这些测试是如何进行的，但由于综述中包含了数据，因此在图例或正文中提供更多关于方法学的细节将非常有用。
2. **图2-5**。应包括一个图例，说明这些图中的红色代表WT，绿色代表低CGG，橙色代表高CGG。此外，图中箱线图外的点是否为异常值而非显著性指标并不明确。关于数据呈现方式的更多信息将有所帮助。此外，为何WT结果的个别数据点并未总是包含在箱线图下方也不清楚。对这些数据是否进行了统计分析？相关性线的R2值，或针对CGG重复长度、年龄的ANOVA分析，都是适合包含在这些结果中的测试，而无需回溯到原始研究手稿。
3. **女性前突变模型小鼠和图3、4**：女性CGG KI模型小鼠在这些测试中也显示出时间处理上的差异，这是一个有趣的观察结果。女性前突变患者通常在拥有一份具有较小重复的FMR1拷贝时表现出较轻的症状，使她们成为致病重复等位基因的杂合子，这归因于X染色体失活和嵌合表达。图3、4中测试的女性小鼠的基因型未标明，应予以明确。性别差异和X染色体失活在与组织病理学内表型的讨论中也被提及，对于不熟悉这一过程及其对疾病影响的读者，需要更多解释。此外，女性小鼠在时间处理上的结果引发了这样一个问题：女性CGG KI小鼠是否已在本文讨论的其他行为任务中进行了测试。
4. **图5**：作者提到Fmr1 KO小鼠并非FXS的完美模型，因为Fmr1表达是通过插入新霉素盒而非通过重复扩展继以启动子和5’UTR高甲基化来消除的，正如人类疾病中那样。因此，将Fmr1 KO数据绘制在/超过200 CGG重复标记处可能是不正确的。这些动物没有任何重复，因此应在不同的尺度上绘制。
5. **分析验证和图7**：图7中提到的两个误分类是否对应于明显的异常动物？回顾那些算法未归类在内的动物数据，并评论它们为何可能在分析中被遗漏，可能是有趣的。
6. **组织病理学内表型**：作者在积累前突变患者和小鼠模型的组织学发现方面做得很好。然而，关于包涵体形成和疾病发病机制当前假设的讨论不足。FXTAS领域有许多理论认为，FMR1 mRNA的增加会导致蛋白质隔离，并可能触发异常蛋白质产物的产生，这些产物可能有助于包涵体的形成。这两个假设的机制数据至少应在此提及。
7. **表1**：所报告的前额皮质和海马体的百分比未解释——这是神经元/胶质细胞中包涵体的百分比吗？此外，应在表中包含CGG重复长度（如可用），因为作者正在评论重复长度与包涵体形成的相关性。
8. **结论，行为内表型**：关于CGG长度、FMR1 mRNA和FMRP表达之间关联的评论需要更多讨论。以某种方式说明CGG重复水平对FMR1 mRNA水平的差异影响，与随CGG重复增加而FMRP表达减少的对比将有所帮助（类似于Brouwer等人2008年生成的表格）。此外，在讨论FXS和Fmr1 KO小鼠背景下的这些内表型时，无FMRP表达、减少的FMRP表达和有毒mRNA的获得性功能之间的差异，都是导致脆性X谱系障碍中独特表型出现的因素（Ludwig等人，2014；Pretto等人，2014）。
9. **未来方向**：呼吁进行更严格的测试以比较小鼠模型和人类患者表型是必要的。然而，在讨论当前模型的局限性时，应指出FXTAS和FXS并非在动物模型普遍失败方面独一无二。小鼠无法完全复现人类神经疾病的状况非常普遍，尤其是在神经退行性疾病中（帕金森病和阿尔茨海默病模型都因未能完全复现临床表型而闻名）。所有模型（包括人类iPS细胞以及简单的系统如蠕虫和果蝇）都存在局限性，但多模型分析的力量可能有望增加从基础科学发现到临床实践转化的可能性。然而，将治疗开发的讨论仅因小鼠模型的基础研究尚未在患者中成功转化为临床试验而视为令人失望，这削弱了该领域在过去十年中所取得的显著进展。

reasons: This review by Michael Hunsaker covers a large body of literature to which he has significantly contributed related to behavioral assay development in Fragile X spectrum disorder mouse models.
The author does a nice job of accumulating histological findings in premutation patients and mouse models.
However, the discussion of current hypotheses around the development of inclusion formation and disease pathogenesis is lacking.

There are many theories in the FXTAS field that the increase of FMR1 mRNA can cause protein sequestration, and may also trigger production of aberrant protein products which could contribute to inclusion formation.
The mechanistic data for both of these hypotheses should be at least mentioned here.
The author includes data from several different published reports to analyze and compare behavioral results in CGG KI premutation model mice to similar tests done in Fmr1 KO animals.
It also addresses shortcomings in the current mouse models of Fragile X spectrum disorders.

The central conclusion of the paper is that the field needs to work towards development of more patient-applicable endophenotypes to allow for successful translation of basic research discoveries to successful therapeutic development.
The call for more rigorous tests to compare mouse models and human patient phenotypes is indeed warranted.
Overall, the article is well written and the title and abstract are appropriate.
More explanation of these behavioral tasks would aid reader comprehension.

Figure 1 was included to help explain how these tests are performed, but as data are included in the review, it would be useful to have more details on methodology in either the figure legends or in the body of the text.
Additionally, it was not clear that the points outside the box plot were outliers and not indicators of significance.
More information about how the data are presented would be helpful.
It’s also unclear why the individual data points for the WT results are not always included below the box plots.
The genotype of the female mice tested in Figures 3, 4, and the text on temporal processing is not indicated, and should be included for clarity.

Sex differences and X-inactivation are also mentioned with the histopathological endophenotype discussion, and warrant more explanation for those unfamiliar with the process and impact that X-inactivation skewing can have on this disorder.

paper_title: Methods used to meta-analyse results from interrupted time series studies: A methodological systematic review protocol
paper_abstract:
Background: Systematic reviews are used to inform healthcare decision making. In reviews that aim to examine the effects of organisational, policy change or public health interventions, or exposures, evidence from interrupted time series (ITS) studies may be included. A core component of many systematic reviews is meta-analysis, which is the statistical synthesis of results across studies. There is currently a lack of guidance informing the choice of meta-analysis methods for combining results from ITS studies, and there have been no studies examining the meta-analysis methods used in practice. This study therefore aims to describe current meta-analysis methods used in a cohort of reviews of ITS studies. 
 Methods: We will identify the 100 most recent reviews (published between 1 January 2000 and 11 October 2019) that include meta-analyses of ITS studies from a search of eight electronic databases covering several disciplines (public health, psychology, education, economics). Study selection will be undertaken independently by two authors. Data extraction will be undertaken by one author, and for a random sample of the reviews, two authors. From eligible reviews we will extract details at the review level including discipline, type of interruption and any tools used to assess the risk of bias / methodological quality of included ITS studies; at the meta-analytic level we will extract type of outcome, effect measure(s), meta-analytic methods, and any methods used to re-analyse the individual ITS studies. Descriptive statistics will be used to summarise the data. 
 Conclusions: This review will describe the methods used to meta-analyse results from ITS studies. Results from this review will inform future methods research examining how different meta-analysis methods perform, and ultimately, the development of guidance.
review_content:
In this protocol, the authors propose to systematically survey methods used to meta-analyze results from interrupted time series (ITS) studies. ITS studies are particularly useful in systematic reviews (SRs) of interventions that cannot be studied using randomized trials (e.g., due to practical, ethical, or legal reasons). Briefly, the protocol plans to identify 100 recent systematic reviews that meta-analyze results from ITS studies and then extract and summarize characteristics of the methods used.

I agree with the authors that we currently know relatively little about the characteristics of methods used in meta-analyses of ITS results. From my point of view, I would like to have evidence that can be used to help design SRs that will meta-analyze ITS results, and to help understand potential weaknesses of such SRs. For example, I would like to have evidence to inform the number of pre- and post-interruption time points that should be required of ITS studies for inclusion in a meta-analysis, and information about whether certain ITS designs and analysis methods lead to excessive bias or imprecision. The protocol says that the resulting work will inform subsequent research that addresses these kinds of questions, using simulation and empirical evaluation. My understanding is that knowing about the landscape of methods that have been used in recent SRs will allow this subsequent work to address relevant questions (e.g., it could allow the authors to design simulation studies that usefully model what is being done in practice).

My review focuses mainly on the conceptual and statistical aspects of the protocol. I cannot comment on other aspects such as the literature search.

I have two "major" criticisms of the protocol:
 1. Because I am more interested in the evidence that the subsequent research will hopefully deliver, I would like to see more detailed thought in this protocol about how the subsequent work will be performed. This should then inform what the product of the present protocol needs to deliver to ensure the success of the subsequent work. Perhaps this has already been thought through in detail and not presented here. However, if this work has not been done, I encourage the authors to do it and update the protocol.
 2. The analysis is not planned in enough detail that it could be implemented without having to make important choices after having seen the data. I think this potentially leads to at two problems. First, being able to choose from among several possible analyses and means of presentation risks introducing bias. Second, more detailed planning at the protocol stage may prevent problems that would otherwise only become apparent while the work is being done. I suggest that the authors substantially revise this section to specify in detail what they will do and how they will report their results, including preparing skeleton tables and/or figures. I think that thinking through these issues at the protocol stage will likely make this and subsequent work (see point 1 above) more efficient, and lead to higher quality papers.
I have the following "minor" comments and suggestions:
 1. I suggest that the abstract is clarified to say that the authors will study the 100 most recent systematic reviews that include ITS analyses (and include the date range), rather than simply saying 100 (or whatever the final sample size is determined to be). My concern when reading the abstract was that the 100 SRs could be chosen arbitrarily, giving rise to potential bias.
 2. It would be useful for the authors to clarify that, with respect to estimating a binomial proportion, their proposed sample size of 100 would give them a worst-case margin of error of plus or minus approximately ten percentage points (i.e., 40.2% to 59.8%), if the population parameter is 50%.
 3. This margin of error is actually quite wide. I wonder if the authors have considered how plausible it is that the population parameter will often be close to the worst-case of 50%, and if so, whether the relatively wide confidence intervals will be informative enough for their subsequent work that will build on this paper?
 4. The sample size of 100 seems to have been chosen under the assumption that a binomial proportion will be estimated for each factor studied (i.e., that each factor will have two levels). However, many of the criteria specified are factors with more than two levels (e.g., the protocol gives the example of three types of outcome that included reviews may study: continuous, count, and rate). Given that, I would encourage the authors to think about the more general case of estimating multinomial proportions. This would require a larger sample size for a worst-case scenario equivalent to that of a binomial distribution. A quick search identified Thompson 19871, which provides a table for estimating sample size for estimating multinomial proportions. Briefly, if the authors want to estimate multinomial proportions with 95% CIs that give a margin or error of plus or minus 10%, that paper shows that the authors should include at least 128 studies (irrespective of the number of levels of the factor studied). However, I encourage the authors to double-check this informal power analysis. The authors would then also need to use an appropriate method to estimate the proportions and their confidence intervals. Given the authors plan to use Stata, I think the correct way to do this is to estimate the proportions using syntax like "mlogit myvar" and then obtain the estimates and their confidence intervals via "margins, predict()", but again I suggest the authors double-check this.
 5. With respect to the "Selection of outcomes" section, it may be useful to rewrite item 1 in terms of "number of model parameters" rather than "number of effect measures". The meaning of the current text was not immediately clear to me.
 6. I suggest the authors plan to extract a little more detail about the methods used to analyze ITS studies, so that this can be used to inform subsequent work. For example, I am interested to know how often "incorrect" model assumptions are assumed, and under what conditions meaningfully incorrect conclusions result from meta-analyses that include ITS results from misspecified models. I'm thinking about the case where an outcome is bounded, where the observed pre- and/or post-interruption levels are close to the bounds, and the analysis assumes an error distribution whose domain includes values outside the bounds. For example, imagine the outcome "percentage of prescriptions with dosage errors", which is bounded to [0%, 100%]. If a normal error distribution is assumed in the ITS analysis, that distribution would incorrectly permit outcomes <0% and >100%. This may not be a problem if the residual standard deviation is small relative to the distance from the mean to the nearest bound, but if the observed data were close to 0% and/or 100% and the residual standard deviation was sufficiently large, the estimate of relative treatment effect estimate might be biased. I would then be interested in knowing, via empirical or simulation work from the planned subsequent research, whether these kinds of errors lead to meaningfully incorrect conclusions when such ITS results are brought into meta-analyses. If this kind of misspecification is uncommon, then perhaps that subsequent work is unnecessary, but my suspicion is that model misspecification (and this misspecification in particular) is actually very common.
 7. I'm also interested in knowing what proportion of ITSs included in meta-analyses assume ITS models that are misspecified in terms of being overly simplistic (e.g., piecewise constant time series with an instantaneous post-intervention step-change). The protocol plans to survey which ITS models are used, but it's not clear whether it aims to judge whether the use is appropriate or not. This is to some extent a judgement about whether particular models are appropriate in particular contexts (all models are approximations of reality), but it would be useful to have a solid evidence base on which to make recommendations for what people should consider when they undertake ITS-based SRs.
 8. The protocol talks about ITS analyses that include versus exclude controls (i.e., where the interruption does not occur), but it's not clear that the protocol will extract data on this. It would be interesting to know what proportion of SRs of ITS studies permit or include uncontrolled ITS results, and ultimately to have some information about whether inclusion of such studies leads to meaningfully incorrect conclusions (I assume it does, though I could imagine that it may be possible to include controlled and uncontrolled ITS results in a meta-regression and still reasonably estimate treatment effect). Similarly, it would be interesting to know how many controls are used (i.e., I assume that ITSs with one control are common but that 10 or 20 controls are quite rare), and then from the subsequent research, the number of controls that SR protocols should specify.
 9. I suggest including the restriction to English as a possible limitation.
I wish the authors success with their research!
paper_title_zh: 用于元分析中断时间序列研究结果的 方法：一项方法学系统综述协议
paper_abstract_zh:
背景：系统评价用于指导医疗决策。在旨在考察组织、政策变化或公共卫生干预措施，或暴露影响的评价中，可能包含中断时间序列（ITS）研究的证据。许多系统评价的核心组成部分是元分析，即跨研究的统计合成。目前缺乏指导选择合并ITS研究结果元分析方法的指南，且尚无研究考察实践中使用的元分析方法。因此，本研究旨在描述一组ITS研究评价中当前使用的元分析方法。

方法：我们将通过检索涵盖多个学科（公共卫生、心理学、教育、经济）的八个电子数据库，识别100篇最新发表（2000年1月1日至2019年10月11日）包含ITS研究元分析的评价。研究选择将由两位作者独立进行。数据提取将由一位作者完成，并对随机样本的评价由两位作者进行。从符合条件的评价中，我们将提取评价层面的详细信息，包括学科、中断类型及用于评估纳入ITS研究偏倚风险/方法学质量的任何工具；在元分析层面，我们将提取结果类型、效应测量指标、元分析方法及用于重新分析单个ITS研究的任何方法。描述性统计将用于总结数据。

结论：本评价将描述用于元分析ITS研究结果的方法。本评价的结果将为未来研究不同元分析方法的性能提供信息，并最终促进指南的发展。
review_content_zh:
在这份协议中，作者们提议系统地调查用于元分析中断时间序列（ITS）研究结果的方法。ITS研究在系统评价（SRs）中特别有用，尤其是那些无法通过随机试验研究的干预措施（例如，由于实际、伦理或法律原因）。简而言之，该协议计划识别100篇最近的系统评价，这些评价对ITS研究的结果进行了元分析，然后提取并总结所使用方法的特点。

我同意作者的观点，即我们目前对用于ITS结果元分析的方法特点了解相对较少。从我的角度来看，我希望有证据可以帮助设计将进行ITS结果元分析的SRs，并帮助理解此类SRs的潜在弱点。例如，我希望有证据来指导ITS研究中应要求包含在元分析中的干预前后时间点的数量，以及关于某些ITS设计和分析方法是否会导致过度偏差或不精确的信息。协议指出，最终的工作将通过模拟和实证评估来回答这类问题。我的理解是，了解近期SRs中使用的方法全景将使后续工作能够解决相关问题（例如，它可以让作者设计出有用地模拟实际操作的模拟研究）。

我的评审主要关注协议的概念和统计方面。我无法对其他方面（如文献检索）发表评论。

我对该协议有两个“主要”批评：
1. 由于我对后续研究可能提供的证据更感兴趣，我希望在协议中看到更多关于如何进行后续工作的详细思考。这应该指导当前协议的产出，以确保后续工作的成功。或许这些已经经过详细思考但未在此呈现。然而，如果这项工作尚未完成，我鼓励作者去做并更新协议。
2. 分析计划的详细程度不足以在看到数据后不做重要选择就能实施。我认为这可能导致两个问题。首先，能够从几种可能的分析和呈现方式中选择，存在引入偏差的风险。其次，在协议阶段进行更详细的规划可能会防止在工作进行时才显现的问题。我建议作者大幅修订这一部分，详细说明他们将做什么以及如何报告结果，包括准备骨架表格和/或图表。我认为在协议阶段思考这些问题可能会使这项和后续工作（见上述第1点）更高效，并导致更高质量的论文。

我有以下“次要”评论和建议：
1. 我建议在摘要中澄清，作者将研究包括ITS分析的100篇最新系统评价（并包括日期范围），而不仅仅是说100篇（或最终确定的样本大小）。我阅读摘要时的担忧是，这100篇SRs可能是任意选择的，从而产生潜在的偏差。
2. 对于估计二项比例，作者提出的100个样本量将给他们一个最坏情况的误差范围，大约为正负十个百分点（即40.2%到59.8%），如果总体参数为50%。
3. 这个误差范围实际上相当宽。我想知道作者是否考虑过总体参数通常接近最坏情况的50%的可能性，如果是这样，相对较宽的置信区间是否足以支持他们后续将基于此论文的工作？
4. 100个样本量的选择似乎是基于假设每个研究的因素将估计一个二项比例（即每个因素有两个水平）。然而，许多指定的标准是具有多于两个水平的因素（例如，协议给出了包括审查可能研究的三个类型结果的例子：连续型、计数型和比率型）。鉴于此，我鼓励作者考虑更一般的情况，即估计多项比例。这将需要一个更大的样本量，以实现与二项分布相当的最坏情况。快速搜索发现了Thompson 19871，该文献提供了估计多项比例样本量的表格。简而言之，如果作者希望以95%置信区间估计多项比例，误差范围为正负10%，那篇论文显示作者应包括至少128项研究（无论因素水平的数量）。然而，我鼓励作者再次检查这种非正式的效力分析。作者还需要使用适当的方法来估计比例及其置信区间。鉴于作者计划使用Stata，我认为正确的方法是使用类似“mlogit myvar”的语法来估计比例，然后通过“margins, predict()”获取估计值及其置信区间，但我再次建议作者再次检查这一点。
5. 关于“选择结果”部分，将第1项重写为“模型参数数量”而不是“效应测量数量”可能更有用。当前文本的含义对我来说并不立即清晰。
6. 我建议作者计划提取更多关于分析ITS研究方法的细节，以便用于指导后续工作。例如，我想知道“不正确”的模型假设有多常见，以及在何种条件下，包含来自错误指定模型的ITS结果的元分析会得出有意义的错误结论。我在考虑一种情况，即结果是有界的，观察到的干预前和/或后水平接近边界，而分析假设的错误分布域包括边界外的值。例如，想象一个结果“处方剂量错误的百分比”，其界限为[0%，100%]。如果在ITS分析中假设正态误差分布，该分布将错误地允许结果<0%和>100%。如果残差标准差相对于均值到最近边界的距离较小，这可能不是问题，但如果观察数据接近0%和/或100%，且残差标准差足够大，相对治疗效果的估计可能会偏倚。然后我将有兴趣知道，通过计划中的后续研究的实证或模拟工作，这类错误是否会导致在将这些ITS结果纳入元分析时得出有意义的错误结论。如果这种错误指定不常见，那么后续工作可能不必要，但我怀疑模型错误指定（尤其是这种错误指定）实际上非常常见。
7. 我还想知道在元分析中包含的ITS中有多少假设了过于简化的ITS模型（例如，具有瞬时干预后阶跃变化的分段常数时间序列）。协议计划调查使用了哪些ITS模型，但不清楚它是否旨在判断使用是否适当。这在一定程度上是对特定模型在特定背景下是否适当的判断（所有模型都是现实的近似），但拥有一个坚实的证据基础来推荐人们在开展基于ITS的SRs时应考虑什么，将是有用的。
8. 协议谈到了包括与不包括控制组的ITS分析（即中断未发生的情况），但不清楚协议是否会提取这些数据。了解有多少比例的ITS研究SRs允许或包括未受控制的ITS结果将是有趣的，并最终了解包含此类研究是否会导致有意义的错误结论（我假设会，尽管我可以想象通过元回归包含受控和未受控制的ITS结果仍能合理估计治疗效果）。同样，了解使用了多少控制组将是有趣的（即我假设使用一个控制组的ITS很常见，但10或20个控制组很少见），然后从后续研究中，SR协议应指定多少个控制组。
9. 我建议将仅限英语作为可能的限制。

祝作者们研究成功！

paper_title: How to incorporate patient and public perspectives into the design and conduct of research
paper_abstract:
International government guidance recommends patient and public involvement (PPI) to improve the relevance and quality of research.  PPI is defined as research being carried out ‘with’ or ‘by’ patients and members of the public rather than ‘to’, ‘about’ or ‘for’ them ( http://www.invo.org.uk/ ). Patient involvement is different from collecting data from patients as participants.  Ethical considerations also differ.  PPI is about patients actively contributing through discussion to decisions about research design, acceptability, relevance, conduct and governance from study conception to dissemination.  Occasionally patients lead or do research.  The research methods of PPI range from informal discussions to partnership research approaches such as action research, co-production and co-learning. 
This article discusses how researchers can involve patients when they are applying for research funding and considers some opportunities and pitfalls.  It reviews research funder requirements, draws on the literature and our collective experiences as clinicians, patients, academics and members of UK funding panels.
review_content:
Thank you for the opportunity to review this article – which I think is an important mile stone publication in the business of patient and public involvement in the activity that prepares and contributes to research applications. This is a timely and useful review of the literature and the experiences of the research authors, one day we might look back and realise that investing in this stage of research yields benefits and savings in research down the line.
I was interested in the reasons for the authors writing this article and was not surprised to see that it was about the conflation of qualitative research and patient and public involvement in research. This article helpfully, and in a practical way helps to ‘de couple’ the most pertinent issues in this domain.
The use of an illustrative example in migraine research helps to bring the review of evidence and discussion in each section to a useful and practical conclusion for the reader, and could be easily re interpreted for their own research context.
It is also a strength in this article that research is considered as both primary studies and research synthesis and reviews, both of which require careful patient and public involvement
Page 3 – in the section How does patient involvement differ from patient participation in research?
“the context and outcomes from listening (to patients) differ. PPI means that researchers are in a continuing and reciprocal relationship with patients and make decisions with them about the research. In qualitative research, researchers listen to patients in order to improve their understanding of a topic”. This is probably the most helpful sentence I have read in a while! The further discussions about the choices of researchers that may or may not include qualitative perspectives in their analysis further underlines that in PPI the power dynamic is different and it is an important difference.
Figure 1 is helpful
I have a problem with the word iterative – and would suggest a plainer language option especially as the rest of the language used in the diagram is of the non-research variety.
Table 2
I struggled with this table maybe because I am not a researcher – I would prefer to see the differences between the two rather than the strengths and limitations of each but can appreciate that for researchers making choices this might be very helpful information and analysis.
Boxes 1 and 2
For an article such as this I think that the contents of Box 2 are more helpful for readers untangling what is meant by PPI in pre funded research and would put Box 1 as a supplementary file – this information is more easily found for a curious researcher and Box 2 really adds value to the article as a whole as authors have collected the (sadly) rather large collection of terminology used in PPI and sought to differentiate it. I like the fact that the authors have stated and used their preferred terminology and articulated the reasons for their choice (partnership approaches).

Table 1
I imagine this could be immensely useful to researchers and it is a useful comparison tool but positioning in the middle of the narrative is a shame I think as it breaks up the flow of reading.

Find out what research questions are priorities for patients
I think that there is a step before initiating priority setting exercises that encompass PPI – increasingly there are published accounts of priority setting that may or may not include the perspectives of patients and the public. There is also an emerging checklist to support the quality assessment of these accounts and specifically the degree of PPI in them
  * Tong A., Sautenet B., Chapman JR., Appraisal checklist used in a systematic review of priority setting partnerships in health research (Currently being reworked as a priority setting reporting checklist and will be renamed REPRISE Checklist).

Consider equity of opportunity, unheard perspectives and health inequalities

This is a particularly important and pertinent section and offers practical advice and ideas for researchers, especially the use of outreach models that offer more scope for addressing these issues more directly, but may put researchers out of their comfort zones.

Consider the potential for bias and conflicts of interest

This feels an underwritten first paragraph. It feels more important to instigate transparency and declaration of financial and other interests for all research participants – than the more in-depth description of the ‘experienced patient?’. Additionally some text about how to manage these conflicts of interests in patients/public may really help readers address this issue.

Agree appropriate funding for patient involvement

There are important considerations here especially around equity of involvement – its good to see these spelled out.

Training for patients involved in research
I was very pleased to see this in the text for this section “For patients new to a PPI role, support to develop their abilities and confidence to express their views and question researchers may be relevant.” A much under-appreciated aspect of PPI, I would suggest that it doesn’t just apply to those new to a role who may find it harder (as am embedded part of the research team) to challenge the research orthodoxy…

Also the training needs to be two way – for research teams as well as involved patients and the public.

Key messages Important questions

I like these but I would include a challenging first question to researchers – ‘Why do they want to do PPI?’
I think that there is an important aspect of self-discovery in PPI in research and it helps to understand self/organisational motivations to doing this preparatory work. These reasons may encompass rational or outcome-based reasons (which the current list addresses) but it is also important to understand motivations on a human and relational level.
paper_title_zh: 如何将患者和公众视角融入研究的设计与实施
paper_abstract_zh:
国际政府指南建议通过患者和公众参与（PPI）来提高研究的关联性和质量。PPI被定义为研究是“与”或“由”患者和公众成员“一起”进行，而不是“对”、“关于”或“为”他们进行（http://www.invo.org.uk/）。患者参与不同于作为参与者从患者那里收集数据。伦理考量也有所不同。PPI涉及患者在研究设计、可接受性、关联性、实施和治理方面的决策中，从研究构思到传播的积极贡献。偶尔，患者会领导或进行研究。PPI的研究方法从非正式讨论到合作研究方法，如行动研究、共同生产和共同学习。

本文讨论了研究者在申请研究资金时如何涉及患者，并考虑了一些机会和陷阱。它回顾了研究资助者的要求，借鉴了文献以及我们作为临床医生、患者、学者和英国资助小组成员的集体经验。
review_content_zh:
感谢您给我机会审阅这篇文章——我认为这是在准备和贡献研究申请活动中患者和公众参与方面的一个重要里程碑出版物。这是一篇及时且有用的文献综述，以及研究作者的经验总结，有朝一日我们可能会回顾并意识到在这一研究阶段进行投资会为后续研究带来益处和节省。

我对作者撰写这篇文章的原因很感兴趣，并不惊讶地发现它是关于定性研究与患者和公众参与研究的混淆。这篇文章以实用且有帮助的方式，帮助“解耦”该领域中最相关的问题。

使用偏头痛研究中的示例有助于将每个部分的证据综述和讨论引向对读者有用且实际的结论，并且可以轻松地重新解释以适应他们自己的研究背景。

这篇文章的另一个优点是，研究被视作既包括初级研究也包括研究综合和综述，这两者都需要谨慎的患者和公众参与。

第3页——在“患者参与研究与患者参与研究的区别是什么？”这一部分中：

“倾听（患者）的背景和结果有所不同。PPI意味着研究人员与患者保持持续且互惠的关系，并与他们共同做出研究决策。在定性研究中，研究人员倾听患者以改善他们对某一主题的理解。”这可能是我在一段时间内读到的最有帮助的一句话！关于研究人员在分析中可能包含或不包含定性视角的进一步讨论，进一步强调了在PPI中权力动态的不同，这是一个重要的区别。

图1很有帮助。

我对“迭代”这个词有疑问，建议使用更平实的语言，尤其是图中的其他语言都是非研究性质的。

表2

我对这个表格感到困惑，可能因为我不是研究人员——我更希望看到两者之间的区别，而不是各自的优点和局限性，但也能理解对于需要做出选择的研究人员来说，这可能是非常有用的信息和分析。

框1和框2

对于这样一篇文章，我认为框2的内容对读者理解预资助研究中PPI的含义更有帮助，我会将框1作为补充文件——这些信息对于好奇的研究人员来说更容易找到，而框2确实为整篇文章增添了价值，因为作者收集了（可惜）相当多的PPI术语，并试图区分它们。我喜欢作者陈述并使用他们偏好的术语，并阐述了选择这些术语的原因（合作方法）。

表1

我想这对研究人员可能非常有用，并且是一个有用的比较工具，但放在叙述中间有点遗憾，因为它打断了阅读的流畅性。

找出对患者来说优先的研究问题

我认为在启动包含PPI的优先级设定练习之前还有一个步骤——越来越多的已发表文献涉及优先级设定，可能包含或不包含患者和公众的视角。此外，还出现了一个支持评估这些文献质量的清单，特别是其中PPI的程度。

* Tong A., Sautenet B., Chapman JR., 用于系统评价卫生研究中优先级设定伙伴关系的评估清单（目前正在重新修订为优先级设定报告清单，并将更名为REPRISE清单）。

考虑机会公平、未被听到的视角和健康不平等

这是一个特别重要且相关的部分，为研究人员提供了实用建议和想法，尤其是使用拓展模型，这些模型提供了更多直接解决这些问题的空间，但可能会让研究人员感到不适。

考虑潜在的偏见和利益冲突

第一段写得不够充分。比起对“有经验的病人？”的深入描述，更重要的是对所有研究参与者实施透明度和财务及其他利益的声明。此外，关于如何管理患者/公众中的这些利益冲突的一些文本，可能会真正帮助读者解决这一问题。

为患者参与提供适当的资金

这里有一些重要的考虑因素，尤其是关于参与的公平性——很高兴看到这些被明确指出。

参与研究的患者培训

我很高兴在这一部分的文本中看到这一点：“对于新参与PPI角色的患者，支持他们发展表达观点和质疑研究人员的能力和信心可能是相关的。”这是PPI中一个被严重低估的方面，我建议这不仅适用于新角色的患者（他们可能觉得更难，因为作为研究团队的一部分），也适用于挑战研究正统观念的人。

此外，培训需要是双向的——既要针对研究团队，也要针对参与的患者和公众。

关键信息 重要问题

我喜欢这些，但我会向研究人员提出一个具有挑战性的第一个问题——“他们为什么想要做PPI？”

我认为在研究中的PPI有一个重要的自我发现方面，它有助于理解自我/组织动机来进行这项准备工作。这些原因可能包括理性或基于结果的原因（当前列表已涵盖），但理解人类和关系层面的动机也很重要。

The use of an illustrative example in migraine research helps to bring the review of evidence and discussion in each section to a useful and practical conclusion for the reader, and could be easily re interpreted for their own research context.

For an article such as this I think that the contents of Box 2 are more helpful for readers untangling what is meant by PPI in pre funded research and would put Box 1 as a supplementary file – this information is more easily found for a curious researcher and Box 2 really adds value to the article as a whole as authors have collected the (sadly) rather large collection of terminology used in PPI and sought to differentiate it.

I imagine this could be immensely useful to researchers and it is a useful comparison tool but positioning in the middle of the narrative is a shame I think as it breaks up the flow of reading.

paper_title: A systematic review of the direct and indirect effects of herbivory on plant reproduction mediated by pollination: theories, methods, and challenges
paper_abstract: Background. Plant reproduction is influenced by the net outcome of plant-herbivore and plant-pollinator interactions. While both herbivore impacts and pollinator impacts on plant reproduction have been widely studied, few studies examine them in concert.
review_content: Reviewer 2 (Anonymous) Basic reporting The organization and flow of the introduction and discussion were somewhat scattered and not always connected to the main point of the methods. Some of this has to do with larger potential issues (i.e. what the purpose of this paper is meant to be; see “General comments” below). But even setting that aside, the organization needs some work. Paragraphs are frequently long, and jump from topic to topic. For example, the first paragraph of the paper covers direct and indirect effects of herbivory, the importance of pollination, potential interactions between herbivores and pollinators, and effects on plant fitness; that’s enough information/topics for three or four paragraphs. >The introduction has been largely re-worked to become more clear and include more detail. There’s also a few language choice problems, including inconsistent use of “direct” and “indirect” (sometimes stated clearly, other times assumed or stated unclearly) and the word “pathways” which seems to have at least three meanings in the introduction (pathways of effect between herbivores and pollinators, different kinds of herbivory, or different classes of interactions such as mutualism vs. antagonism). Also, the introduction uses the hypothesis in Figure 1 as part of the justification for the paper, but doesn’t ever directly talk about that figure or its implied hypothesis/es. >We have gone through and clarified our word choice as well as better outlined Figure 1 in the introduction. Raw data have been supplied and are mostly labeled well, though some of the values, abbreviations, and column headings are unintuitive. For example, using “number of pollinators” = “100” to denote an entire community was studied. The accessory documents define all of these well enough, but there may be changes that would make the data easier to understand without having to reference additional documents. >Good point, we have renamed several of the column names and changed the “100” value used. I like Figure 1, and I think it could serve as a hypothesis for a path analysis in future research. However, on two different computer screens the green color used for some arrows was very difficult to tell apart from gray or black; when printed in grayscale, it was even worse. >Thank you very much for pointing this out as this was less clear on our screens. We have changed the colouring by both increasing the contrast and making it more colour-blind and gray-scale friendly. Figure 4 is very information-dense, which makes it somewhat difficult to parse – but the figure legend explains things fairly well. Figure 3 was the figure I struggled the most with. I understand what it’s trying to show (and how), but the lines don’t always connect with the species names and it’s frequently hard to tell what the lines are connecting or pointing to. It’s also not obvious what order the interactions are listed in; it’s not alphabetical by species names. >Thank you for the suggestions, this figure was not easy to edit since the algorithm by default orders the species so as to minimize crossing of lines, but we have attempted to make it more user-friendly by re-arranging nodes and adjusting the lines using a different program and custom algorithm. The tables in both the paper and in the supplemental documents were hard to tell where horizontal dividers belonged. Additionally, text in each column isn’t necessarily justified vertically in the same way across rows. For example, in Table 1, the term “Root Herbivory” is justified higher in the cell than its definition in the next column, which makes it hard to read as a cohesive row. There needs to be either space between each row or horizontal lines added. >We have added spaces between horizontal lines and adjusted justifications. Experimental design I had trouble deciding what the main purpose or question of this paper was meant to be; see my comments below in “General comments.” There was very little in the way of experimental design and even less about how the analysis was completed. The methods section was only one short paragraph long, and focus on how papers were found and sorted, with no information about what data were taken from those papers or how those data were further analyzed. Overall, methods and results focus mostly on qualitative information, with less interest in analytical or technical information. >Since this was not a meta-analysis, most of the data collected was qualitative. However, we did include more information on what was extracted from each study. Validity of the findings It’s not always entirely clear how the authors decided which paper goes in which category, especially when it comes to things like simulated herbivory/florivory or studies with multiple species or studies that didn’t measure reproduction etc. I tried to parse through some of the data based on citations I’m familiar with, and frequently I would have put different data points in their table. This makes it difficult to know if the summary of what kinds of studies have or haven’t been published is accurate. I can’t tell if this is a matter of providing consistent, logical definitions for each data choice, or if the data itself are too subjective to be interpreted analytically. >We were concerned that you found that you would have parsed things differently, so we went through to re-check the studies and tried to make it more clear in our definitions how we came to each term. Previously we had grouped several categories together when defining study methods, by re-parsing them into their original categories, they should be more logical. The main conclusion of the paper seems to be that herbivores effect pollinators (directly and/or indirectly) which in turn can affect plant pollination success. As a conclusion, this feels weak; this is something that is already well known by ecologists in this field, and probably assumed by ecologists in related fields. Additionally, that conclusion doesn’t tie back to the results in this paper (looking at where more studies are needed, for example). This conclusion is valid, but it doesn’t serve either the purpose of the paper or the scientific audience of a paper like this. >We have reworked our discussion and conclusions to try to make our main findings clearer. Comments for the Author I’ve read this paper several times through in preparing to write this review. This general topic is one of great interest to me. There have been previous reviews that touch on how herbivory and/or florivory specifically affect pollination and (potentially) plant reproduction, but they are all several years old now. I think there is room to have a review that talks about what we know and what we have left to learn on the topic. However, I’m not convinced this paper fills that role. The methods and results of this paper focus on the number of papers published in this field, pointing out what kind of studies are most and least common. But the methods and results don’t attempt to summarize the kinds of results those papers found. Meanwhile, the introduction and discussion provide a cursory summary of the results from those papers (as you would find in the introduction section of an original research paper, for example) but doesn’t really put them in the context of how many articles of each type have been published. This makes the paper feel like two separate things, neither of which is completely satisfying. I think the authors may need to think about what they’re trying to accomplish with this piece. If their goal is mainly to point out the gaps in terms of where papers are or are not being published, that can be done in a much more concise manner (a “Note” article, for example) that could summarize the information presented in the methods and results section of this paper as a sort of call to arms for researchers. This could be of interest to anyone familiar with the field, and might provide a jumping-off point for new research project ideas. However, an article of that type would need only limited review of results from those previous papers (since the “results” would be how many and what kind of articles are being published); in that case, the information currently in the introduction and discussion of this paper would be greatly reduced to a couple of paragraphs for context. If the main goal with this paper is to review the results from previous herbivore-plant-pollinator studies, then there should be less focus on how many papers have been published and more focus on what the results of those papers were. This may or may not include a meta-analysis, if you want a more analytical approach to the data. Even a traditional review, however, could provide new insights into what the common trends are in this field, with room to point out remaining gaps in our knowledge. In a review paper of this type, the results and methods section as currently written would go away (though there may be mention of numbers of studies in the discussion) and the current introduction/discussion would need to be expanded and reorganized around common themes in the results from published papers. As I said before, there have been reviews that do this already for this topic, but they’re all a decade or so old by now, so there’s probably room for a new one – especially if you focus on what’s been added to the literature more recently. Overall, while there is a lot of good information in this paper, its current format is somewhat confusing and unsatisfying.
paper_title_zh: "对植食性动物通过授粉对植物繁殖的直接和间接影响的系统综述：理论、方法与挑战"
paper_abstract_zh: 背景。植物繁殖受植物-食草动物和植物-传粉者相互作用净结果的影响。尽管食草动物对植物繁殖的影响和传粉者对植物繁殖的影响都已得到广泛研究，但很少有研究将它们结合起来进行考察。
review_content_zh:
审稿人2（匿名）

**基本报告**

引言和讨论的组织和流程有些散乱，并不总是与方法部分的主要观点相连接。部分原因在于一些潜在的较大问题（即本文的目的究竟是什么；见下文“总体评论”）。但即使抛开这一点，文章的组织结构仍需改进。段落通常较长，且话题跳跃。例如，文章的第一段涵盖了植食性的直接和间接效应、授粉的重要性、植食性动物与传粉者之间的潜在相互作用以及对植物适应性的影响；这些信息/话题足以构成三到四个段落的内容。>引言部分已经进行了大量修改，以使其更加清晰并包含更多细节。此外，还存在一些语言选择问题，包括“直接”和“间接”使用的不一致性（有时表述清晰，有时假设或表述不清）以及“途径”一词在引言中至少有三种含义（植食性动物与传粉者之间的效应途径、不同类型的植食性以及不同类别的相互作用，如互利共生与对抗）。此外，引言部分使用图1中的假设作为论文的部分依据，但并未直接讨论该图或其隐含的假设。>我们已经仔细检查并澄清了我们的用词，并在引言中更好地概述了图1。

原始数据已经提供，并且大部分标签清晰，但某些数值、缩写和列标题不够直观。例如，使用“传粉者数量”=“100”来表示整个群落被研究。辅助文档对这些定义得足够清楚，但可能需要一些改动，以便在不参考额外文档的情况下更容易理解数据。>很好的建议，我们已经重新命名了几个列标题，并更改了使用的“100”值。

我喜欢图1，我认为它可以用作未来研究中路径分析的假设。然而，在两台不同的电脑屏幕上，用于某些箭头的绿色非常难以与灰色或黑色区分；当以灰度打印时，情况更糟。>非常感谢您指出这一点，因为这在我们的屏幕上也不够清晰。我们已经通过增加对比度并使其更适合色盲和灰度打印来更改了颜色。

图4信息密度很高，这使得它有些难以解析——但图例解释得相当清楚。图3是我最费解的一张图。我理解它试图展示的内容（以及如何展示），但线条并不总是与物种名称相连，且常常难以分辨线条连接或指向的内容。此外，相互作用的排列顺序也不明显；它不是按物种名称的字母顺序排列的。>感谢您的建议，这张图不容易编辑，因为算法默认按最小化线条交叉的方式排列物种，但我们已经尝试通过使用不同的程序和自定义算法重新排列节点和调整线条，使其更加用户友好。

论文和补充文档中的表格难以分辨水平分隔线的位置。此外，每列中的文本并不一定在行之间垂直对齐。例如，在表1中，“根植食性”一词在单元格中的对齐位置高于下一列中的定义，这使得将其作为一个整体行阅读变得困难。需要在每行之间添加空间或水平线。>我们已经添加了水平线之间的空间并调整了对齐方式。

**实验设计**

我难以确定本文的主要目的或问题是什么；见下文“总体评论”中的评论。实验设计方面的内容非常少，关于分析如何完成的内容更少。方法部分仅有一段简短的文字，重点在于如何查找和分类论文，而没有关于从这些论文中提取了哪些数据或这些数据如何进一步分析的信息。总体而言，方法和结果部分主要关注定性信息，对分析或技术信息的兴趣较少。>由于这不是一篇元分析，收集的大部分数据是定性的。然而，我们确实包括了更多关于从每项研究中提取了什么信息的内容。

**结论的有效性**

作者如何决定将哪篇论文归入哪个类别并不总是完全清楚，尤其是在涉及模拟植食性/花食性或涉及多个物种的研究或未测量繁殖的研究等方面。我尝试根据我熟悉的引用解析部分数据，发现我常常会将不同的数据点放入他们的表格中。这使得难以确定已发表或未发表的研究类型的总结是否准确。我无法判断这是否是一个为每个数据选择提供一致、逻辑定义的问题，还是数据本身过于主观，无法进行统计分析。>我们担心您发现您会以不同的方式解析事物，所以我们重新检查了研究，并试图在定义中更清楚地说明我们如何得出每个术语。之前我们在定义研究方法时将几个类别组合在一起，通过将它们重新解析为原始类别，它们应该更加逻辑化。

本文的主要结论似乎是植食性动物影响传粉者（直接和/或间接），进而可以影响植物授粉成功。作为一个结论，这显得有些薄弱；这是该领域生态学家已经熟知的事情，相关领域的生态学家可能也认为是理所当然的。此外，这个结论并没有与本文的结果（例如，查看哪些方面需要更多研究）联系起来。这个结论是有效的，但它既不符合本文的目的，也不符合这类论文的科学受众。>我们已经重新编写了讨论和结论部分，以使我们的主要发现更加清晰。

**对作者的评论**

在准备撰写这篇评论的过程中，我已经通读这篇文章多次。这个一般性话题是我非常感兴趣的。之前已有一些综述涉及植食性或花食性如何具体影响授粉和（潜在的）植物繁殖，但它们现在都已经有些年头了。我认为有必要有一篇综述来讨论我们对这个话题的了解以及我们还有哪些需要学习的内容。然而，我不确定这篇文章是否填补了这个角色。本文的方法和结果部分侧重于该领域已发表论文的数量，指出哪些类型的研究最常见和最不常见。但方法和结果并没有试图总结这些论文发现的结果类型。与此同时，引言和讨论部分提供了这些论文结果的简要总结（例如，就像在原创研究论文的引言部分中那样），但并没有真正将其置于每种类型文章发表数量的背景下。这使得文章感觉像是两个独立的部分，没有一个完全令人满意。

我认为作者可能需要思考他们试图通过这篇文章实现什么目标。如果他们的主要目标是指出论文发表或不发表的地方的差距，这可以以更简洁的方式进行（例如，一篇“简讯”文章），可以总结本文方法和结果部分呈现的信息，作为对研究者的号召。这可能对熟悉该领域的任何人都有兴趣，并可能为新研究项目想法提供起点。然而，这类文章只需要对那些先前论文的结果进行有限的回顾（因为“结果”将是发表了多少以及哪些类型的文章）；在这种情况下，本文引言和讨论中的信息将大幅缩减为几段背景介绍。

如果本文的主要目标是回顾先前植食性动物-植物-传粉者研究的结果，那么应该减少对已发表论文数量的关注，而更多地关注这些论文的结果是什么。这可能包括或不包括元分析，如果您希望对数据采取更分析性的方法。即使是传统的综述，也可以提供对该领域常见趋势的新见解，并指出我们知识中的剩余空白。在这类综述文章中，目前编写的结果和方法部分将消失（尽管在讨论中可能会提到研究的数量），而当前的引言/讨论部分需要围绕已发表论文结果的常见主题进行扩展和重新组织。正如我之前所说，已经有一些综述对这一主题进行了这样的处理，但它们现在都已经过去十年左右了，所以可能还有空间进行新的综述——尤其是如果您专注于近年来文献中新增的内容。

总体而言，尽管本文包含大量有用信息，但其当前格式有些令人困惑且不令人满意。

reasons: As a conclusion, this feels weak; this is something that is already well known by ecologists in this field, and probably assumed by ecologists in related fields.
This conclusion is valid, but it doesn’t serve either the purpose of the paper or the scientific audience of a paper like this.
However, I’m not convinced this paper fills that role.

If the main goal with this paper is to review the results from previous herbivore-plant-pollinator studies, then there should be less focus on how many papers have been published and more focus on what the results of those papers were.
Even a traditional review, however, could provide new insights into what the common trends are in this field, with room to point out remaining gaps in our knowledge.
Paragraphs are frequently long, and jump from topic to topic.

There’s also a few language choice problems, including inconsistent use of “direct” and “indirect” (sometimes stated clearly, other times assumed or stated unclearly) and the word “pathways” which seems to have at least three meanings in the introduction (pathways of effect between herbivores and pollinators, different kinds of herbivory, or different classes of interactions such as mutualism vs. antagonism).
Raw data have been supplied and are mostly labeled well, though some of the values, abbreviations, and column headings are unintuitive.
Figure 4 is very information-dense, which makes it somewhat difficult to parse – but the figure legend explains things fairly well.
Figure 3 was the figure I struggled the most with.
I understand what it’s trying to show (and how), but the lines don’t always connect with the species names and it’s frequently hard to tell what the lines are connecting or pointing to.
It’s also not obvious what order the interactions are listed in; it’s not alphabetical by species names.
The tables in both the paper and in the supplemental documents were hard to tell where horizontal dividers belonged.
Additionally, text in each column isn’t necessarily justified vertically in the same way across rows.
For example, in Table 1, the term “Root Herbivory” is justified higher in the cell than its definition in the next column, which makes it hard to read as a cohesive row.
The organization and flow of the introduction and discussion were somewhat scattered and not always connected to the main point of the methods.
Paragraphs are frequently long, and jump from topic to topic.
I had trouble deciding what the main purpose or question of this paper was meant to be; see my comments below in “General comments.”

The methods section was only one short paragraph long, and focus on how papers were found and sorted, with no information about what data were taken from those papers or how those data were further analyzed.
The methods and results of this paper focus on the number of papers published in this field, pointing out what kind of studies are most and least common.

Meanwhile, the introduction and discussion provide a cursory summary of the results from those papers (as you would find in the introduction section of an original research paper, for example) but doesn’t really put them in the context of how many articles of each type have been published.
This makes the paper feel like two separate things, neither of which is completely satisfying.
Overall, while there is a lot of good information in this paper, its current format is somewhat confusing and unsatisfying.

paper_title: BioHackathon series in 2013 and 2014: improvements of semantic interoperability in life science data and services
paper_abstract: Publishing databases in the Resource Description Framework (RDF) model is becoming widely accepted to maximize the syntactic and semantic interoperability of open data in life sciences. Here we report advancements made in the 6th and 7th annual BioHackathons which were held in Tokyo and Miyagi respectively. This review consists of two major sections covering: 1) improvement and utilization of RDF data in various domains of the life sciences and 2) meta-data about these RDF data, the resources that store them, and the service quality of SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language (SPARQL) endpoints. The first section describes how we developed RDF data, ontologies and tools in genomics, proteomics, metabolomics, glycomics and by literature text mining. The second section describes how we defined descriptions of datasets, the provenance of data, and quality assessment of services and service discovery. By enhancing the harmonization of these two layers of machine-readable data and knowledge, we improve the way community wide resources are developed and published.  Moreover, we outline best practices for the future, and prepare ourselves for an exciting and unanticipatable variety of real world applications in coming years.
review_content:
The authors report on the many activities conducted under the umbrella of the BioHackathons 2013 and 2014. While there are recurring intellectual threads, most notably a focus on support for RDF, the manuscript is really a collection of reports of the progress made by each of the different subgroups involved in these events. I admire the work that must have gone into fitting each of these individual efforts into a coherent narrative, and this is a very useful historical document of those efforts.

I do have some suggestions below where I think the manuscript could be improved - primarily to help developers and users put this work into context. Most of these are are not critical flaws, however, and I would leave to the authors' discretion how they wish to respond to these comments and suggestions.

The one issue I think is critical for acceptance is the explanation of Figure 1 (see below).

One recurring issue is the ambiguity of the reference time frame, both for the starting and stopping points of the work described. This is important since the report covers work that took place 5-6 years in the past, a long time ago in the world of bioinformatics.

With respect to the starting point, the use of present tense makes it unclear in many passages whether the authors are describing the state of software as of 2013/2014, or today. To avoid confusion, I would recommend either fixing the relevant passages throughout (I list some of them below) or clarify upfront that the state of affairs of the software tools and resources described is as of 5-6 years ago, which in many cases will no longer be accurate.

Regarding the stopping point, it is not clear if the progress described reflects what was accomplished during the event, up until the next biohackathon, or some other time point.

This is perhaps a larger ask, but I wanted as a reader to know where these efforts stand today. Putting the work in context of the progress since would take a weakness of the manuscript (ie. reporting on older work) and turn it into a virtue (evaluating the impact each of these efforts had on their fields with the benefits of a few years of hindsight). Perhaps this could be summarized by a "where-are-they-now" table.

In addition, there are a number of claims made, particularly regarding tool performance, without supporting evidence provided. In some cases, these might be from subjective assessments, which is fine as long as that is clear. But subjective or not, the lack of evidence makes the claims difficult to evaluate. I point some of these passages out below.

COMMENTS BY SECTION:

ABSTRACT

"an exciting and unanticipatable variety of real world applications in coming years" - this is an odd statement given that several years have already passed.

INTRODUCTION

"To fully utilize open data in life sciences, semantic interoperability and standardization of data are required to allow innovative development of applications" - while it may be true, this claim is not directly supported. A weaker claim might be more justified.

IMPROVEMENT AND UTILIZATION OF RDF DATA IN LIFE SCIENCES"
"RDF ... is becoming widely accepted" - can the other cite support for this claim?

GENOMIC INFORMATION

FIGURE 1 - needs further explanation via a caption and/or legend. What do the colors represent, and the different types of lines? The use of URLs deserves explanation - especially the one to a google doc.

IDENTIFIERS FOR SEQUENCES AND ANNOTATIONS

I couldn't quite figure out what I was supposed to understand about the conceptual differences among the identifier models.

TOOLS FOR SEMANTIC GENOME DATA

"To support these efforts we have collaborated with DDBJ, UniProt, and the EBI RDF group to develop ontologies for representing locations and annotations of genome sequences and used these developments for all prokaryotic genomes and, later, eukaryotic genomes"
- this passage seems redundant with the descriptions above. Also, the use of "we" here and in next sentence appears to be legacy text referring to only the TogoGenome participants.

JBrowse on RDF was comparable in performance to typical RDB back-end - it would be good if the authors could support that claim with some of the data obtained.

The sections "Visualization of semantic annotations in JBrowse" and "TogoGenome" are somewhat redundant with each other. I recommend merging.

INTERMINE
"An area that needs work, and is receiving attention," - is this still true 5-6 years later?

"Implement a simple adaptor allowing, as described above, JBrowse to request data directly from InterMine RESTful web services" If this was actually described above, I missed it.

TEXT-MINING

I would personally find a screenshot of the text annotations in JBrowse much more interesting than the current Figure 2, which is exactly what you'd expect it to look like and doesn't provide evidence for the *performance* claim above.

PROTEIN STRUCTURES AND EXPRESSIONS

"the Worldwide Protein Data Bank (wwPDB) will abolish the conventional PDB format" and "wwPDB will start assigning protein chain identifiers, which will also be encoded as URIs in the wwPDB/RDF." 2016 is three years ago, so if this has already been accomplished, this should be in past tense.

"Recently, the mzTab data exchange format was introduced" - recently meaning 2014?

"the "omics" group in the BioHackathon 2014 made the first steps towards the development of the ProteomeXchange Interface (PROXI) for protein expression data exchange59." - my impression is that this effort has evolved considerably since 2014. If true, it would be valuable to put this into context for how the technology is used currently by the ProteomeXchange consortium.

"integration of the two corpora, CRAFT and GRO, into PubAnnotation, demonstrated significantly improved utility" - is there supporting evidence for this claim?

"Access to consistent, high-quality metadata is critical to finding, understanding, and reusing scientific data - this is the core of the FAIR Data Principles83." - it's odd to reference this manifesto of principles that postdates the hackathons by at least two years. This would be less awkward if there was a table or section devoted to developments *since* the 2014, i.e. "where are they now?"

DATASET METADATA

"The resulting guidelines, finalized under the auspices of the W3C Semantic Web for Health Care and the Life Sciences Interest Group (HCLSIG)" - there's no link or citation given here.

The 4th pgph redundantly includes the same coverage list: "..elements of description, identification, versioning, attribution, provenance, and content summarization."

"The group is currently evaluating the specification with implementations for dataset registries such as Identifiers.org50 and IntegBio Database Catalog, as well as Linked Data repositories such as Bio2RDF84." - update on progress since 2014?

W2C link appears to be dead, but a paper was published in 2016. I get the impression that there was further work on this post-hackathon not mentioned here.

VOID FOR INTERMINE AND UNIPROT

The relationship of prior work on VOiD (if any) to the outcome from the hackathon is not clear to me.

"there are now InterMine databases available" - is "now" as of writing, or as of the time of the hackathon?

The VoID file [for Uniprot] is updated every release in synchrony with our production" - replace use of "our" which I presume refers to the Uniprot team and not to the collaborative team of authors here.

SCHEMA>ORG AND RDFA FOR BIOLOGICAL DATABASES

what's "NIBIOHN"?

NANOPUBLICATIONS

A more explicit explanation of the relationship between NANOPUBLICATIONS and the overarching topic of PROVENANCE would be helpful.

"n-quads" - please explain or provide a reference.

"At the time of writing, YummyData has collected data for about a year" - what is the time of writing?

CONCLUSION

"The NBDC RDF portal launched in 2015 complements the above resources..." - again, this would be appropriate for a "where are they now?" section.

"will be addressed in the upcoming BioHackathons" - they have been held annually since 2014, so it is odd to not mention what *was* addressed in subsequent events. And I hope those reports will be published in a more timely fashion!
paper_title_zh: 2013和2014年BioHackathon系列活动：生命科学数据和服务语义互操作性的改进
paper_abstract_zh: 在资源描述框架（RDF）模型中发布数据库正逐渐被广泛接受，以最大化生命科学中开放数据的语法和语义互操作性。本文报道了在东京和宫城分别举行的第六届和第七届年度BioHackathon所取得的进展。本综述包括两个主要部分：1）在生命科学各个领域中RDF数据的改进和利用，以及2）关于这些RDF数据的元数据、存储它们的资源以及SPARQL协议和RDF查询语言（SPARQL）端点的服务质量。第一部分描述了我们在基因组学、蛋白质组学、代谢组学、糖组学以及通过文献文本挖掘中如何开发RDF数据、本体和工具。第二部分描述了我们是怎样定义数据集的描述、数据的来源以及服务和服务发现的质评估。通过增强这两层机器可读数据和知识的协调，我们改进了社区范围内资源开发和发布的方式。此外，我们概述了未来的最佳实践，并为未来几年激动人心且不可预见的各种现实世界应用做好准备。
review_content_zh:
作者们报告了在2013年和2014年BioHackathons大旗下开展的多项活动。尽管存在一些反复出现的智力线索，尤其是对RDF支持的关注，但该手稿实际上是对参与这些活动的各个不同子小组所取得进展的集合报告。我钦佩将这些个人努力融入连贯叙述中的工作，这是一份非常宝贵的历史文献。

以下是我认为手稿可以改进的一些建议——主要是帮助开发者和用户将这些工作置于背景中。大多数这些建议并非关键性缺陷，不过，我将如何回应这些评论和建议留给作者自行决定。

我认为接受的关键问题是图1的解释（见下文）。

一个反复出现的问题是参考时间框架的模糊性，包括所描述工作的起始和结束点。这很重要，因为报告涵盖了5-6年前的工作，在生物信息学领域已经是很久以前的事了。

关于起始点，使用现在时态使得许多段落中不清楚作者是在描述2013/2014年的软件状态，还是今天的。为了避免混淆，我建议要么修正相关段落（我在下面列出了一些），要么提前澄清所描述的软件工具和资源的状况是5-6年前的，这在许多情况下可能已不再准确。

关于结束点，不清楚所描述的进展是反映了活动期间所取得的成果，直到下一个biohackathon，还是某个其他时间点。

这可能是一个更大的要求，但作为读者，我想知道这些努力目前的状况。将工作置于自那以来的进展背景中，可以将手稿的弱点（即报告较旧的工作）转变为优点（评估这些努力在各自领域的影响，并受益于几年的事后洞察）。或许可以通过一个“现状如何”的表格来总结。

此外，还有一些主张，尤其是关于工具性能的，没有提供支持证据。在某些情况下，这些可能是主观评估，只要明确这一点是可以的。但无论主观与否，缺乏证据使得这些主张难以评估。我在下面指出了一些这样的段落。

按章节评论：

摘要

“在未来几年中将出现令人兴奋且不可预测的多种现实世界应用”——鉴于已经过去几年，这是一个奇怪的说法。

引言 "为了充分利用生命科学中的开放数据，需要实现数据的语义互操作性和标准化，以允许应用的创新开发"——尽管这可能属实，但这一主张并未得到直接支持。一个较弱的论点可能更有道理。

"改进和利用生命科学中的RDF数据"
"RDF……正逐渐被广泛接受"——其他文献能否支持这一主张？

基因组信息

图1——需要通过标题和/或图例进一步解释。颜色代表什么，不同类型的线条又代表什么？URL的使用需要解释——尤其是指向谷歌文档的那个。

序列和注释的标识符

我无法完全理解不同标识符模型之间的概念差异。

语义基因组数据工具

"为了支持这些努力，我们与DDBJ、UniProt和EBI RDF小组合作，开发了用于表示基因组序列位置和注释的本体，并利用这些开发成果应用于所有原核基因组，随后又应用于真核基因组"——这一段落似乎与上述描述重复。此外，这里和下一句中使用的“我们”似乎是遗留文本，仅指TogoGenome的参与者。

JBrowse on RDF在性能上与典型的RDB后端相当——如果作者能用获得的一些数据支持这一主张会更好。

“在JBrowse中可视化语义注释”和“TogoGenome”这两节内容彼此有些重复。建议合并。

INTERMINE
“一个需要改进且正在受到关注的领域”——5-6年后这还成立吗？

“实现一个简单的适配器，如上所述，使JBrowse能够直接从InterMine RESTful网络服务请求数据。”如果这在上文已有描述，我错过了。

文本挖掘

我个人觉得JBrowse中文本注释的截图比当前的图2更有趣，图2完全符合预期，并未提供上述性能主张的证据。

蛋白质结构和表达

“世界蛋白质数据库（wwPDB）将废除传统的PDB格式”和“wwPDB将开始分配蛋白质链标识符，这些标识符也将作为URI编码在wwPDB/RDF中。”2016年是三年前，所以如果这已经完成，应该使用过去时态。

“最近，mzTab数据交换格式被引入”——最近是指2014年？

“2014年BioHackathon的‘组学’小组迈出了开发蛋白质表达数据交换接口（PROXI）的第一步。”——我的印象是自2014年以来这一努力已有了显著发展。如果属实，将其置于当前ProteomeXchange联盟如何使用该技术的背景中将很有价值。 "将CRAFT和GRO两个语料库整合到PubAnnotation中，显著提高了其效用" - 是否有支持这一主张的证据？

"访问一致、高质量的元数据对于查找、理解和重用科学数据至关重要 - 这是FAIR数据原则83的核心。" - 引用这份至少比黑客马拉松晚两年发布的宣言原则显得有些奇怪。如果有一个表格或章节专门介绍2014年以来的发展情况，即“他们现在如何？”，则会显得不那么尴尬。

数据集元数据

“在W3C语义网健康护理和生命科学兴趣小组（HCLSIG）的指导下最终确定的指导方针” - 这里没有给出链接或引用。

第四段冗余地包含了相同的覆盖列表：“...描述元素、识别、版本控制、归属、来源和内容总结。”

“该小组目前正在评估该规范在数据集注册机构（如Identifiers.org50和IntegBio数据库目录）以及关联数据存储库（如Bio2RDF84）中的实施情况。” - 2014年以来的进展更新？

W2C链接似乎已失效，但2016年发表了一篇论文。我得到的印象是，黑客马拉松之后还有进一步的工作，但这里没有提及。

INTERMINE和UNIPROT的VOID

先前对VOiD的工作（如果有的话）与黑客马拉松的结果之间的关系对我来说并不清楚。

“现在有InterMine数据库可用” - “现在”是指写作时，还是指黑客马拉松时？

“Uniprot的VoID文件每次发布都与我们的生产同步更新” - 请替换“我们的”一词，我推测这指的是Uniprot团队，而不是这里的作者协作团队。

SCHEMA.ORG和RDFA用于生物数据库

“NIBIOHN”是什么？
