paper_title: One step further in palaeontology: A nonlinear finite element analysis review Jordi Marcé-Nogué
paper_abstract: Finite Element Analysis (FEA) is no longer a new technique in the fields of palaeontology, anthropology, and evolutionary biology. It is nowadays a well-established technique within the virtual functional-morphology toolkit. However, almost all the works published in these fields have only applied the most basic FEA tools i.e., linear materials in static structural problems. Linear and static approximations are commonly used because they are computationally less expensive, and the error associated with these assumptions can be accepted. Nonetheless, nonlinearities are natural to be used in biomechanical models especially when modelling soft tissues, establish contacts between separated bones or the inclusion of buckling results. The aim of this review is to, firstly, highlight the usefulness of non-linearities and secondly, showcase these FEA tool to researchers that work in functional morphology and biomechanics, as non-linearities can improve their FEA models by widening the possible applications and topics that currently are not used in palaeontology and anthropology.
review_content: Reviewer 2 (Emily Rayfield) Basic reporting The review considers the use of non-linear approaches in finite element modelling, with the aim of introducing the potential of these approaches to a palaeontological audience. This is clear in the introduction, as is the motivation of the study. Later, the 'palaeontological audience' is more broadly interpreted as palaeo, archaeology, and zoology, which is, in reality, the audience the review is aimed at. There is scope for a review of this nature. As the author points out, most studies and most previous reviews have focused on linear static methods in the bio- and historical sciences. Yet in medical sciences, non-linear approaches are more commonplace. The review will be of interest to the field. For the most part a description of the mathematical and computatinal underpinnings are matched to the relevant biological structure or approach (although see below where these links could be stronger or clearer). Experimental design In a short review such as this it's impossible to capture the breadth of the field. However the examples chosen do span taxonomic groups and different approaches. I don't have any concerns about this. The references seem adequately cited. Organisation seems logical. I thank the reviewer for being supportive. Validity of the findings So this is where I have the majority of comments. My overwhelming feeling when finishing reading the manuscript was, we can do all of this, but *should* we do all of this, and do we *need* to do all of this? The objective of this paper is to raise these kinds of questions in the readers. I am just bringing on the table some forgotten modelling to the community. Then, are the researchers who should decide if they want to include them or not. This is because one thing that's missing from the whole review is a discussion of validation. The non-linear approaches are introduced, there’s a discussion of which materials, tissues or structures and loading scenarios might lend themselves to a non-linear approach – I have no qualms about this. But, do we need to introduce this level of complexity to get the results we need? There are some mentions of this in the text, but the danger is that a reader may interpret this paper to think that one must apply these approaches to get a more accurate and realistic result. The medical community and the examples I provide can be an example of how improve our models. Of course, that not always is true, but this is the decision one should take when creates a model. I use a lot of linear models in comparative models because I am aware that more complexity is not necessary, but also, I included complexity in other works because I think that it is necessary for the sake of the results. The paper aims also to raise some critical spirit among the researchers of the paleo community. But is this really the case? In most instances we don’t know. Take the PDL as an example. We could define the PDL as a contact surface, but do we need to define this as a contact surface to get the most accurate results? Do we need to actually introduce such complexity into our models? Likewise, we could introduce muscles as non-linear features, but actually some elastic linear studies have got really quite good results using subject specific models, detailed material properties and applying muscle forces directly to the model. Take Panagiotopoulou et al. 2017 (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0944200616301805) as a good example of a linear elastic model where computational strain values that match those measured in vivo with a high degree of accuracy. Explores the role of the PDL again using a linear elastic noncontact approach (Panagiotopoulou et al. 2019) https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fbioe.2019.00269/full This review needs to acknowledge the lack of understanding of how much introducing non-linear methods improve accuracy or predictability of models. This is an example of a linear assumption that can be accepted because the value of the forces applied is very small. So, PDL works as a linear material under small loads. Certainly, in the text I wrote regarding linear models of soft tissue that "can be an appropriate simplification if this is validated experimentally". But, what about using the same model for another research/work where bigger forces need to be applied? The non-linear behaviour of the PDL need to be considered, so in this case we need to be aware that PDL must be modelled as an hyperelastic material because if we model it as a linear model, results will not fit. The orthodontic community uses hyperelastic laws in their works to model PDL, so, why we cannot use them? We cannot predict the behaviour of PDL in fossils irrespective if we model them as linear or non-linear, so why we cannot model PDL with data from non-linear models instead from linear models? The amount of error and uncertainty would be the same. Or, why we cannot run experimental tests in living relatives to capture the non-linear behaviour instead of capturing the linear behaviour? It is well-known that, for example, PDL should be modelled in a general form as a non-linear material. So, it would be more accurate. The text aims to open this debate and to draw attention that the lack of understanding of the community can be solved watching what other bio communities are doing. Sections on plastic deformation (line 151 onwards) and buckling (line 189 onwards). These sections need to acknowledge that plastic behaviours in materials such as dentine or enamel represent the extremes of the loading environment rather than everyday behaviour. Included Likewise, simulations of buckling in structures such as limb bones would also represent extreme loading conditions at the point of critical failure. Neither would be useful simulations to understand everyday loading behaviours. Further on the point of buckling, I’m not convinced that a rigid upright column is the appropriate model to represent a multi-jointed musculoskeletal system such as the limb. Why for example might it be useful to test if the bones of dinosaurs or mastodons are affected by buckling? Surely this would tell us the maximum loads that could be experienced but equally this could be achieved simply by running simulations of individual limb bones and seeing which one reaches critical failure first? In both this context of plastic deformation and buckling the review needs to be careful not to mislead the reader that such non-linear simulations would represent everyday behavioural functions. As it is explained in the text, buckling reduces the capacity of the strength of the structure because it appears in a lower value than the yield stress and the fracture stress that defines the strength of the material. Therefore, this cannot be achieved simply by running linear, elastic simulations under different scenarios of individual limb bones and seeing which one reaches critical failure first. Because the critical failure obtained in both methods is not the same and does not need to be proportional. This is the reason why I am suggesting buckling as an alternative analysis when we have, for example, leg bones in heavy dinosaurs. As Currey (2011) states: "Failure of a structure may be described as becoming unfit for its purpose, whatever that may be, and does not necessarily imply fracture. Bone may fail for not being stiff enough, through buckling, either Euler or local". I tried to explain better in the text. Of course, that a rigid upright column is not the appropriate model to represent a multi-jointed musculoskeletal system such as the limb, but it is illustrative of how buckling can be affected by geometrical and material parameters. The Euler's critical force is only possible to be calculated under this simple circumstances. For complex geometries as bones, we need to use computational methods such as FEA. So, the example of the column is an illustrative simplification, but the message of the manuscript is to use it in FEA with real geometries. More specific comments: Line 19 - assuming linear elasticity in bone is not a simplification for most loading scenarios (avoiding large loads). The sentences do not refer particularly to bone (or to the material properties). There are other non-linearities a part of the material ones such as contacts, large deformations, etc... that make this sentence true. Lines 23-25 – also we use linear models because we understand the properties of these materials better than those with non-linear properties? And, we’ve performed validation studies in some models that show that the results are appropriate for the question of interest. Same answer above applies. Lines 76 to 104. There’s some repetition in these three paragraphs (see comments on my PDF). I tried to improve the text. Lines 279 to 282. Picking up on the question of muscles again, if it's not clear how soft tissues can accurately be predicted in fossils, then surely we should be avoiding modelling these soft tissues using non-linear material properties because this has the potential to introduce more error to our models? We cannot predict the behaviour of muscles in fossils irrespective if we model them as linear or non-linear. What we do is use the material properties of a close living relative and in this case, probably non-linearities are closer to the real behaviour than the elastic simplification. Line 330 – section 5.4. I think the section on using contacts could be more nuanced. For example, I think it's a good idea to include contact surfaces when modelling multi bone structures with joints and range of motion, such as the carpal bones of the wrist or the bones of the foot (as examples presented here). However, going back to my original point about the PDL, do we need to model adjacent materials that lack articulations as contact surfaces? Studies that have tried to model sutures in different ways for example using contact surfaces or springs, have shown variable results. It goes back to the point about whether introducing more complexity is really worth the extra time and effort and computational power and if this is going to produce a more accurate result, and indeed whether a more accurate result is actually warranted by the question at hand. A good example of this is modelling fossils, where we do not know material property values or the true extent of soft tissues and therefore muscle input forces with a high degree of accuracy. Is it therefore necessary to introduce other complex features when we know our results will not represent the absolute stresses and strains student structure in life? I come back to a sentence I wrote in the introduction of the manuscript: "mathematical nonlinearities are natural in physical models and the assumption of linearity and staticity is a simplification of reality to make the problem easy to solve". So, the inclusion of this complexity is to create more accurate models to have more realistic results. Regarding the question if it is necessary to introduce complex features, I want to also come back to something that it is written in the text: "This text does not want to spread an incorrect idea regarding the use of supposedly more accurate non-linear models. In fact, the use of linear low computational approaches without nonlinearities can also be of utility to understand the behaviour of the biological bodies under analysis. Certainly, the majority of the FEA works that are including fossils are based in studying bones as a reconstruction of the fossil remains, which can be modelled successfully using linear elastic material properties and solved using a static analysis under small strains and displacements, therefore, without non-linearities" because "The aim of this text is to highlight the value of non-linearities when they can be of utility, or they are needed to improve the knowledge we have". According to the first reviewer, "Non-linear FEA is hardly ever used in zoo/paleo modelling, and while it is often unnecessary, sometimes its inclusion will be essential. This review provides an overview of these situations" because "people are generally unaware that they could or should be using non-linear methods". Instead, the medical community is using them a lot and for this reason I am just including their citations. The aim of this manuscript is open the debate the reviewer 2 is raising here. So, I am happy to see that it has effect. The final decision if it is necessary to include or not the non-linearities should be yours, the researchers. I have a few different comments on the figures. I’ve added these to pdf. The reviewer has also provided an annotated manuscript as part of their review I included the changes proposed by the reviewer in the attached PDF FIGURES I included the changes in the captions of the figures the reviewers proposed. However, I di not modify figure 5 with a more "biological" example because the simplicity of two surfaces being in contact each other is what the figure aims to show. A more biological example will involve more complex geometries, losing the pedagogical meaning of the figure. For biological examples, I forward the reader to the citations of the text. Also in this figure: It is difficult to label the types of contacts with a more generic name since other software use similar wording (see for example: https://knowledge.autodesk.com/support/inventor/learn-explore/caas/CloudHelp/cloudhelp/ 2020/ENU/Inventor-Help/files/GUID-4CAFC652-873B-4709-B107-D39A399FCE8D-htm. html) For this reason, I am explaining the meaning of each contact type (which is the important part of the text) and then, I warn that depending on the software this label could potentially change or, maybe the type of contact is not available.
paper_title_zh: 古生物学再进一步：非线性有限元分析综述  Jordi Marcé-Nogué
paper_abstract_zh: 有限元分析（FEA）在古生物学、人类学和进化生物学领域已不再是一项新技术。如今，它已成为虚拟功能形态学工具包中的一项成熟技术。然而，在这些领域发表的几乎所有研究都仅使用了最基本的FEA工具，即线性材料在静态结构问题中的应用。线性静态近似之所以普遍使用，是因为它们在计算上成本较低，且这些假设相关的误差是可以接受的。尽管如此，非线性在生物力学模型中是自然应用的，尤其是在模拟软组织、建立分离骨骼间的接触或包含屈曲结果时。本综述的目的是，首先强调非线性的实用性，其次向从事功能形态学和生物力学研究的人员展示这些FEA工具，因为非线性可以通过拓宽目前在古生物学和人类学中尚未应用的潜在应用和主题，来改进他们的FEA模型。
review_content_zh:
审稿人2（艾米丽·雷菲尔德）

基本报告

该综述考虑了非线性方法在有限元建模中的应用，旨在向古生物学者介绍这些方法的潜力。这在引言中是明确的，研究的动机也是如此。随后，“古生物学者”被更广泛地解释为古生物学、考古学和动物学，实际上这正是该综述的目标读者。此类综述有其存在的空间。正如作者所指出的，大多数研究和之前的综述都集中在生物和历史科学中的线性静态方法上。然而在医学科学中，非线性方法更为常见。该综述将对领域内产生兴趣。在大多数情况下，数学和计算基础的描述与相关的生物结构或方法相匹配（尽管如下所述，这些联系可以更强或更清晰）。

实验设计

在如此简短的综述中，不可能涵盖该领域的广度。然而，所选的例子确实涵盖了不同的分类群和不同的方法。我对这一点没有疑虑。参考文献似乎引用得当。组织结构似乎合理。感谢审稿人的支持。

结果的可靠性

这是我有最多评论的地方。读完手稿后，我的强烈感觉是，我们可以做所有这些，但*应该*做所有这些吗？我们*需要*做所有这些吗？本文的目标是引发读者对这些问题的思考。我只是将一些被遗忘的建模方法带到社区中来。然后，研究人员应该决定是否要包含它们。这是因为整个综述中缺少的一个讨论是验证。非线性方法被引入，讨论了哪些材料、组织或结构以及加载场景可能适合非线性方法——我对这一点没有异议。但是，我们需要引入这种程度的复杂性来获得所需的结果吗？文中提到了一些相关内容，但危险在于，读者可能会解读本文认为必须应用这些方法以获得更准确和现实的结果。医学界和我提供的例子可以作为如何改进我们模型的示例。当然，这并不总是正确的，但这是在创建模型时应该做出的决定。我在比较模型中使用了大量的线性模型，因为我知道更多的复杂性是不必要的，但在其他工作中，我也引入了复杂性，因为我认为这对于结果来说是必要的。本文还旨在在古生物学者群体中引发一些批判精神。但情况真的是这样吗？在大多数情况下我们并不清楚。以PDL为例。 我们可以将牙周韧带（PDL）定义为接触面，但为了获得最准确的结果，我们是否需要将其定义为接触面？我们是否真的需要将这种复杂性引入我们的模型中？同样，我们可以将肌肉引入为非线性特征，但实际上一些弹性线性研究在使用特定受试者模型、详细的材料属性并将肌肉力直接应用于模型时，已经获得了相当好的结果。以Panagiotopoulou等人2017年的研究（https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0944200616301805）为例，这是一个线性弹性模型的良好示例，其中计算应变值与体内测量值高度吻合。再次探讨了使用线性弹性非接触方法（Panagiotopoulou等人2019年）的PDL作用（https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fbioe.2019.00269/full）。这篇综述需要承认对引入非线性方法在多大程度上提高模型准确性或可预测性的理解不足。这是一个线性假设的示例，可以接受，因为施加的力值非常小。因此，在小载荷下，PDL表现为线性材料。当然，在我关于软组织线性模型的文本中写道，“如果通过实验验证，这可能是一个适当的简化”。但是，如果在另一项研究中需要施加更大的力，使用相同的模型会怎样？需要考虑PDL的非线性行为，因此在这种情况下，我们必须意识到PDL必须被建模为超弹性材料，因为如果我们将其建模为线性模型，结果将不匹配。正畸学界在其工作中使用超弹性定律来建模PDL，那么为什么我们不能使用它们？无论我们将PDL建模为线性还是非线性，我们都无法预测化石中PDL的行为，那么为什么我们不能用非线性模型的数据而不是线性模型的数据来建模PDL？误差和不确定性的量将是相同的。或者，为什么我们不能在活体亲属中进行实验测试以捕捉非线性行为，而不是捕捉线性行为？众所周知，例如，PDL应该被普遍建模为非线性材料。这样会更准确。本文旨在开启这一辩论，并引起注意，社区的理解不足可以通过观察其他生物社区的做法来解决。关于塑性变形（从第151行开始）和屈曲（从第189行开始）的章节。这些章节需要承认，牙本质或牙釉质等材料中的塑性行为代表了加载环境的极端情况，而不是日常行为。同样，肢体骨骼等结构的屈曲模拟也代表了临界失效点的极端加载条件。两者都不适用于理解日常加载行为。 关于屈曲问题，我并不认为一个刚性的直立柱模型适合代表如肢体这样的多关节肌肉骨骼系统。例如，为什么测试恐龙或乳齿象的骨骼是否受屈曲影响是有用的呢？这当然会告诉我们可能经历的最大负荷，但同样，这也可以通过简单地运行单个肢体骨骼的模拟，并观察哪一个首先达到临界失效来实现？在塑性变形和屈曲的这两种情况下，综述需要小心，不要误导读者认为这类非线性模拟能代表日常行为功能。正如文中所述，屈曲降低了结构的强度能力，因为它出现在低于屈服应力和定义材料强度的断裂应力的值。因此，这不能仅仅通过在不同情景下运行单个肢体骨骼的线性弹性模拟，并观察哪一个首先达到临界失效来实现。因为两种方法获得的临界失效并不相同，也不需要成比例。这就是为什么我建议在分析重恐龙的腿骨等情况下，将屈曲作为一种替代分析方法。正如Currey（2011）所言：“结构的失效可以描述为不适合其目的，无论其目的是什么，并不一定意味着断裂。骨骼可能因为不够坚硬而失效，通过屈曲，无论是欧拉屈曲还是局部屈曲。”我在文本中试图解释得更清楚。当然，一个刚性的直立柱并不是代表如肢体这样的多关节肌肉骨骼系统的适当模型，但它可以说明几何和材料参数如何影响屈曲。欧拉临界力只有在这些简单情况下才能计算。对于如骨骼这样的复杂几何形状，我们需要使用如有限元分析（FEA）这样的计算方法。因此，柱子的例子是一个说明性的简化，但手稿的要点是将其应用于具有真实几何形状的FEA中。更具体的评论：第19行——假设骨骼的线性弹性在大多数加载情景下（避免大负荷）并不是简化。这些句子并没有特别指骨骼（或材料属性）。除了材料非线性外，还有其他非线性，如接触、大变形等，使这句话成立。第23-25行——我们也使用线性模型，是因为我们更了解这些材料的属性，而不是那些具有非线性属性的材料的属性吗？并且，我们在一些模型中进行了验证研究，表明结果适合感兴趣的问题。上述答案同样适用。第76至104行。这三段中有一些重复（见我PDF上的评论）。我试图改进文本。第279至282行。 再次回到肌肉的问题上，如果尚不清楚如何准确预测化石中的软组织，那么我们当然应该避免使用非线性材料属性来模拟这些软组织，因为这有可能给我们的模型引入更多误差。无论我们将肌肉模拟为线性还是非线性，我们都无法预测化石中肌肉的行为。我们所做的是使用一个近亲生物的材料属性，在这种情况下，非线性可能比弹性简化更接近真实行为。第330行——第5.4节。我认为关于使用接触面的部分可以更加细致。例如，我认为在模拟具有关节和活动范围的多骨结构时，包括接触面是个好主意，如手腕的腕骨或足骨（如本文所举的例子）。然而，回到我最初关于PDL的观点，我们是否需要将缺乏关节的相邻材料模拟为接触面？试图以不同方式模拟缝合线的研究，例如使用接触面或弹簧，已经显示出不同的结果。这回到了一个观点，即引入更多复杂性是否真的值得额外的时间和努力以及计算能力，以及这是否会产生更准确的结果，实际上，更准确的结果是否确实由手头的问题所需要。一个很好的例子是模拟化石，我们不知道材料属性值或软组织的真实范围，因此无法高度准确地输入肌肉力。因此，在我们知道结果不会代表生物体在生活中的绝对应力和应变的情况下，引入其他复杂特征是否必要？我回到手稿引言中写的一句话：“数学非线性在物理模型中是自然的，线性假设和静态性是对现实的简化，以使问题易于解决。”因此，包含这种复杂性是为了创建更准确的模型以获得更现实的结果。关于是否有必要引入复杂特征的问题，我还想回到文本中提到的一点：“本文不希望传播关于使用所谓更准确的非线性模型的错误观念。事实上，使用没有非线性的线性低计算方法也可以有助于理解所分析生物体的行为。 当然，大多数包含化石的有限元分析（FEA）工作都是基于研究骨骼作为化石遗骸的重建，这些可以通过使用线性弹性材料属性成功建模，并使用小应变和小位移下的静态分析求解，因此，没有非线性，因为“本文的目的是强调非线性在它们可能有用或需要改进我们现有知识时的价值”。根据第一位审稿人的意见，“非线性FEA在动物学/古生物学建模中几乎从未使用，尽管它通常是不必要的，但有时其包含将是至关重要的。这篇综述概述了这些情况”，因为“人们通常不知道他们可以或应该使用非线性方法”。相反，医学界大量使用这些方法，因此我只是引用了他们的文献。本文的目的是开启审稿人2在此提出的辩论。所以，我很高兴看到它产生了效果。是否需要包含非线性的最终决定应由你们研究人员决定。我对图表有一些不同的评论。我已经将这些添加到PDF中。审稿人还提供了一份带注释的手稿作为其评审的一部分，我将审稿人提出的更改包含在附件的PDF图表中。我按照审稿人的建议更改了图表的标题。然而，我没有用更“生物学”的例子修改图5，因为两个表面相互接触的简单性正是该图要展示的内容。一个更生物学的例子将涉及更复杂的几何形状，失去了该图的教诲意义。对于生物学的例子，我将读者引向文本中的引用。同样在这张图中：很难用更通用的名称标记接触类型，因为其他软件使用类似的措辞（例如：https://knowledge.autodesk.com/support/inventor/learn-explore/caas/CloudHelp/cloudhelp/2020/ENU/Inventor-Help/files/GUID-4CAFC652-873B-4709-B107-D39A399FCE8D-htm.html）。因此，我解释了每种接触类型的含义（这是文本的重要部分），然后，我警告说，根据软件的不同，这个标签可能会改变，或者，也许该接触类型不可用。

paper_title: Causal Reinforcement Learning: A Survey
paper_abstract: Reinforcement learning is an essential paradigm for solving sequential decision problems under uncertainty. Despite many remarkable achievements in recent decades, applying reinforcement learning methods in the real world remains challenging. One of the main obstacles is that reinforcement learning agents lack a fundamental understanding of the world and must therefore learn from scratch through numerous trial-and-error interactions. They may also face challenges in providing explanations for their decisions and generalizing the acquired knowledge. Causality, however, offers notable advantages by formalizing knowledge in a systematic manner and harnessing invariance for effective knowledge transfer. This has led to the emergence of causal reinforcement learning, a subfield of reinforcement learning that seeks to enhance existing algorithms by incorporating causal relationships into the learning process. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive review of the literature in this domain. We begin by introducing basic concepts in causality and reinforcement learning, and then explain how causality can help address key challenges faced by traditional reinforcement learning. We categorize and systematically evaluate existing causal reinforcement learning approaches, with a focus on their ability to enhance sample efficiency, advance generalizability, facilitate knowledge transfer, mitigate spurious correlations, and promote explainability, fairness, and safety. Lastly, we outline the limitations of current research and shed light on future directions in this rapidly evolving field.
review_content:
**Summary Of Contributions:**
This paper is entitled "Causal Reinforcement Learning: A Survey". It introduces some background concepts on causality and RL, presents a broad definition of the umbrella term causal RL, and presents an overview of existing works grouped by the challenges they try to address: sample efficiency, transfer, spurious correlation, and other considerations (explainability, fairness, safety). The paper concludes with open problems and future directions for the field. The paper's main contribution is: - a broad survey of existing works - establishing connections via a problem-oriented taxonomy

**Strengths And Weaknesses:**
### Strengths - the survey compiles a wide range of existing works in causal RL, which is a significant contribution in itself - the problem-oriented categorization of these works also makes sense and I believe can be useful to newcomers and practitioners ### Weaknesses - the introduction (Section 1) is problematic. I find it is very poor at motivating what causality can bring to the field of RL, and is in fact quite misleading. It does not even mention the requirements and restrictions of most causal RL approaches (prior causal knowledge), but rather presents all of the beliefs of the field ("causality can significantly improve the robustness and interpretability of machine learning models") as indisputable facts. Such a one-sided view is ok for an opinion paper, but it is particularly problematic for a survey paper aimed at newcomers. Instead of providing a fair overview of the promise, challenges and open questions, it perpetuates the delusion that causality is a magic tool that will solve all of RL's problems, which is in the end detrimental to the field. See my detailed comments. - the background (Section 2) contains technical ambiguities and inconsistencies (definition of causal graph, initial state as exogenous variable). It proposes the MDP setting as a unified framework to discuss causal RL approaches, which makes little sense as this setting alleviates most of the difficulties causal RL approaches try to tackle, such as confounding or transfer to new tasks (see my detailed comments). - the sections "Why causality helps [...]" are too assertive, in the sense that they state "causality helps" (indisputable fact) "here is why", without any nuance (see my comments on Section 3.2). Again, presenting such strong assertions without nuance about the limitations in a survey paper is I think harmful. - the structure of the paper is redundant and confusing at times (e.g., 6.1.1 and 6.4.1, see detailed comments) - the content of the section "Open Problems and Future Directions" does not fit the description, as it mostly enumerates further existing works that do not fit the proposed taxonomy. I'd suggest to re-work that section and better sort what are actual open problems and future directions. Even better, a section named "Limitations and future directions" would make more sense, as in general all of the presented problems (sample efficiency, transfer, spurious correlation, explainability, fairness, safety) are still open problems. I have also noted some relevant recent works on causal RL that are missing from the survey: - Gun et al. ICML 2022 Provably Efficient Offline Reinforcement Learning for Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes - Pace et al. ICML 2023 Delphic Offline Reinforcement Learning under Nonidentifiable Hidden Confounding - Gasse et al. TMLR 2023 Using Confounded Data in Latent Model-Based Reinforcement Learning ### Detailed comments - p1 "emerge" -> typo - p2: "causality can significantly improve the robustness and interpretability of machine learning models" -> I find this whole paragraph rather ambiguous and not well motivated. The difference between "pure data-driven" methods, "causality" and "causal inference" is not clear. In the proposed example with scurvy, a classic online RL algorithm such as REINFORCE or Q-learning does solve the problem optimally, without the explicit need for causality. The problem here relies on the data at hand, experimental data versus observational data. Causality offers a framework / a set of tools to express this problem, but not necessarily a way to solve it. Based on purely observational data, causal inference is in general impossible. I find that this paragraph does a very poor job at explaining the essence of the problem, and rather lures readers into the delusion that causality is a generic tool that can just be applied on top of any ML model, and will improve their robustness as by magic. This is especially problematic for a survey paper targeted at newcomers in the field. - p2 "in most RL studies, agents are only allowed to intervene in action variables" -> why is this a problem? For which purpose is this a problem? The general goal in RL is to find an optimal policy for an agent that can act only using the action variables. What would be the benefit of knowing what would happen if one could act on other variables, if in the end these variables are not actionable? It seems like the narrative here is "RL needs causality because RL can not learn causality". What is missing here is, why would a full causal model benefit RL in the first place? Again, I find this paragraph unconvincing and very poor at motivating what causality can bring to existing RL algorithms. - p2 "In contrast, with causal RL, you would begin by analyzing the causal relationships and making informed assumptions" -> Same comment as before. This example is misleading. Traditional (online) RL requires no assumptions and leads to an optimal policy, given enough data is collected. Causal RL as described here requires either causal assumptions, which can be wrong (superstition, wrong beliefs), or causal knowledge, which in turn requires experimental data to acquire. Causal reasoning on top of wrong assumptions can be harmful. This is a key limitation to all causal RL methods, and deserves to be part of the discussion. Again, I find this narrative quite confusing, very one-sided, and misleading towards the belief that causal inference always brings benefits to RL. - p3 "the essence, implications, and opportunities of causal RL" -> what about the limitations? - p4 "definitionn" -> typo - p4 "when the parent set PA(Vi) is too small" -> I don't see how small parent sets might violate a Markovian property - p4 "the omitted variables influence multiple variables in V" -> what is an omitted variable? Is it the same as an exogenous variable? - p4 "Markovian property" -> has not been defined yet. Which Markovian property? - p4 "latent variables" -> are latent variables equivalent to exogenous variables in your SCM formulation? I find it confusing to refer to exogenous, omitted and latent variables without clarification. - p5 Figure 3a -> I find this representation of probability distributions hard to read. How do these pie charts represent probability distributions? - p5 "sailors would be" -> would have been - p8 figure 4 -> In the POMDP setting the policy does not have access to the full state, and can not be represented as $do(a \sim \pi(\dot | s_t))$. POMDPs require a different formalism for the policy. As a suggestion, it would be simpler to present only the POMDP regime, which is more general, and derive the MDP regime as a special case (with constraint $O_t=S_t$). Also, one of the main problems that causality tries to address is confounding, which does not happen in the MDP setting. One more reason to focus on POMDPs. - p8 "initial state can be considered an exogenous variable" -> I do not follow this reasoning. How can the state, reward and action be endogenous variables, and $S_0$ be an exogenous variable at the same time? Is $S_0$ observed or not to decide on the initial action $A_0$? Is this the MDP or the POMDP setting? - p9 "On-policy RL directly learns the causal effects of actions on the outcome from interventional data." -> Then is on-policy RL already a causal RL method? Is causality only useful in the offline setting? - p9 "Fortunately [...] we can identify the desired causal effect through certain causal reasoning techniques" -> this is not always true (identifiability problem). This sentence is misleading. - p10 "Why Causality Helps Improve Sample Efficiency" -> The paper's title suggests a survey paper, but this section really sounds like an opinion piece. The general tone is 'causality improves sample-efficiency, without question, and here is why'. This is a strong statement, which I find is put forward without due caution. I understand the belief expressed in this section, but I find it problematic that it is presented here as a general truth. The usefulness of causal approaches for sample-efficiency, and for RL in general, yet remains to be demonstrated in the general setting, both in theory and in practice. I strongly suggest changing the tone in this section, and add more nuance, e.g., "How can causality improve sample efficiency?" - p10 "causality helps reduce the complexity" -> This is the motivation for a family of approaches, not a general truth. It should be presented as such. "most / many causal RL approaches are motivated by the idea that exploiting the true causal structure of the problem will reduce the complexity of learning, and thus improve sample efficiency" - p10 "non-causal methods often demonstrate lower efficiency compared to causal RL methods" -> Again, this assertion is not a universal truth. I'd suggest a less assertive tone: "in some controlled settings, non-causal methods have been shown to demonstrate lower efficiency compared to causal RL methods", or "(Seitzer et al., 2021) show that methods exploiting causal influence for exploration improve sample-efficiency in robotic manipulation tasks" - p10 Section 3.3 -> I like this section, which gives a comprehensible summary of existing works. The sub-sections however are highly redundant to the discussion in Section 3.2. I would suggest to merge Sections 3.2 and 3.3 for readability, or simply remove Section 3.2 all together. - p22 Section 6 "Considerations Beyond Return" -> I find the structure of this section confusing. 6.1.1 "Leveraging Causality for Explainability" is redundant with 6.4.1 "Explainable Reinforcement Learning with Causality", then 6.2.2 "Leveraging Causality for Fairness" is redundant with 6.4.2 "Fair Reinforcement Learning with Causality", same with 6.3.2 and 6.4.3 about Safety. I suggest to merge these sections. - p27 Section 7 -> This section is named "Open Problems and Future Directions", but in reality it is a continuation of the survey of existing works. How is "7.2 Causality-aware Multitask and Meta Reinforcement Learning" an open problem, while "4.3.1 Generalize to Different Environments" or "4.3.2 Generalize to Different Tasks" are not? This structure does not maker much sense to me. - p31 "causal RL is a promising method" -> Causal RL is not a single method, as stated in definition 2.3.

**Requested Changes:**
Critical: - rework the narrative, in particular the introduction, and present a more nuanced view of causal RL with a less assertive tone - fix the technical ambiguities and inconsistencies - make it clearer what are the motivations (hopes, beliefs) for causal RL, what has been achieved and demonstrated so far (successes), what are the costs and limitations of causal RL, and what remains to be done Strengthen the work: - improve the structure of the paper - add missing works to the survey

**Claims And Evidence:**
No

**Audience:**
Yes

**Rebuttal Comments:**
Response to Reviewer H8ZM: Thank you very much for your thorough review and insightful feedback on our manuscript! We have carefully addressed each of your points and made necessary revisions, as outlined below: > (C2, 3, 4) Improve the introduction's clarity on the role and limitations of causality in RL. To better illustrate the motivation of causal RL and the intersection of causality and RL, we have replaced the scurvy example with real-world applications more closely related to reinforcement learning (robot manipulation, medical treatment, and autonomous driving). We have included a new figure (figure 1 on page 2) and enhanced the discussion in Section 1 to better analyze the limitations inherent in traditional reinforcement learning (the second paragraph on page 2). In the revised manuscript, we have also highlighted the consequences of wrong assumptions as one of the issues that causal RL needs to investigate, and added additional discussion in Section 7.1 (the second paragraph on page 27). > (C7) How small parent sets might violate a Markovian property? Here we are quoting Judea Pearl's discussion of the Markov assumption in [1], Chapter 2.2: "If a set $\text{PA}_i$ in a model is too narrow, there will be disturbance terms that influence several variables simultaneously and the Markov property will be lost." That is to say, exogenous variables affecting more than one endogenous variable exist in this case. Therefore, $V_i$ may not remain independent of its non-descendant variables when conditioned on $\mbox{\textbf{PA}}(V_i)$. > (C8, 10) Relationship among omitted variables, exogenous variables and latent variables. In the revised manuscript, we have clarified the connection between these three terms (the second paragraph on page 4). Omitted variables is an informal term that denotes factors that are excluded from the system for abstraction in this context. SCM refers to these factors as exogenous variables, which influence the values of the endogenous variables. If there are exogenous variables affecting more than one endogenous variable, the model loses the Markov property. If we explicitly express such variables as latent variables in the causal graph, the Markov property can be restored. > (C9) Definition of Markovian property. In the context of SCM, this implies that $V_i$ is independent of its non-descendant nodes when conditioned on its parents $\mbox{\textbf{PA}}(V_i)$. > (C11, 13) Improve Figure 3a and Figure 4. We have enhanced the caption for Figure 3a (page5) in the revised manuscript and modified Figure 4 to focus on POMDPs (page 8). > (C14) Why the initial state can be considered an exogenous variable? Thank you for pointing this out. We have removed this confusing statement. > (C15) Is on-policy RL already a causal RL method? On-policy RL can sometimes learn the total effects of actions on the outcome from interventional data, but it does not directly constitute a causal RL approach. It is also incorrect that causal RL is only useful in the offline setting. Even in the online setting, there are still many issues that require knowledge about causality, such as how to collect intervention data more efficiently, how to transfer acquired knowledge, and how to analyze discrimination that occurs in a decision-making process. Lots of the research presented in Sections 3 to 6 is conducted in the online setting, as indicated in Tables 1-4. > (C17, 18, 19) Adjust the assertive tone of the sample efficiency section. We have revised the section names and texts you mentioned to provide a more nuanced perspective that includes discussions on limitations. Thank you very much for your valuable opinions! > (C20, 21) Merge redundant sections for clarity We have merged the sections according to your comments for readability. > (C22) Revise Section 7 to better reflect the content. In the revised manuscript, we have changed the name of Section 7 to "Limitations and future directions", as you suggested, and added Section 7.1 (page 27), dedicated to outlining the limitations of current methods. In addition, we have explicitly emphasized that the problems discussed in Sections 3-6 remain open for further investigation (the last paragraph on page 26). > (C24) Additional relevant works on addressing confounding bias We have incorporated discussions on the first two references (Guo et al., 2022 and Pace et al., 2023 ) you pointed out (the third paragraph on page 16). The third reference (accepted by TMLR on Aug, 2023) is an updated version of a paper we have already cited. Therefore, we have updated the reference to reflect this new version. > (C1, 5, 6, 12, 16, 23) Typos and edits. Thank you for pointing out these issues, we have revised and checked the paper according to your comments. Once again, we would like to express our gratitude for your valuable insights, which have undoubtedly contributed to the improvement of our work. [1] Pearl, Judea. _Causality_. Cambridge university press, 2009.
paper_title_zh: 因果强化学习：综述
paper_abstract_zh: 强化学习是解决不确定性环境下序贯决策问题的重要范式。尽管在近几十年取得了许多显著成就，但将强化学习方法应用于现实世界仍然充满挑战。主要障碍之一是强化学习代理缺乏对世界的基本理解，因此必须通过大量的试错交互从头开始学习。它们还可能面临为其决策提供解释和将所学知识泛化的挑战。然而，因果关系通过系统化地形式化知识并利用不变性实现有效知识转移，提供了显著优势。这催生了因果强化学习，这一强化学习的子领域旨在通过将因果关系融入学习过程来增强现有算法。在本综述中，我们对这一领域的文献进行了全面回顾。我们首先介绍了因果关系和强化学习的基本概念，然后解释了因果关系如何帮助解决传统强化学习面临的关键挑战。我们对现有的因果强化学习方法进行了分类和系统评估，重点关注它们在提高样本效率、增强泛化能力、促进知识转移、减轻虚假相关性以及提升可解释性、公平性和安全性方面的能力。最后，我们概述了当前研究的局限性，并展望了这一快速演变领域的未来方向。
review_content_zh:
**贡献总结：**
本文题为“因果强化学习：综述”。介绍了因果性和强化学习（RL）的背景概念，提出了因果RL这一总括性术语的广泛定义，并概述了现有工作，按其试图解决的挑战进行分类：样本效率、迁移、虚假相关性以及其他考虑因素（可解释性、公平性、安全性）。文章最后总结了该领域的开放问题和未来方向。本文的主要贡献是：- 对现有工作的广泛综述 - 通过问题导向的分类建立联系。

**优点和缺点：**
### 优点 - 该综述汇集了因果RL领域的广泛现有工作，这本身就是一项重要贡献 - 这些工作的问题导向分类也合乎逻辑，我相信对新手和从业者都很有用 ### 缺点 - 引言（第1节）存在问题。我认为它在激励因果性对RL领域带来的贡献方面非常薄弱，实际上相当误导。它甚至没有提及大多数因果RL方法的要求和限制（先验因果知识），而是将领域内的所有信念（“因果性可以显著提高机器学习模型的鲁棒性和可解释性”）作为无可争议的事实呈现。这种片面的观点在观点性文章中尚可接受，但对于面向新手综述性文章来说尤其成问题。它没有提供一个关于前景、挑战和开放问题的公平概述，而是延续了因果性是解决RL所有问题的神奇工具的错觉，这对领域最终是有害的。详见我的详细评论。 - 背景（第2节）包含技术上的模糊性和不一致性（因果图的定义，初始状态作为外生变量）。它提出将MDP设置作为讨论因果RL方法的统一框架，这几乎没有意义，因为这种设置减轻了因果RL方法试图解决的大部分困难，如混杂因素或新任务的迁移（详见我的详细评论）。 - “为什么因果性有帮助 [...]" 各节过于断言，它们陈述“因果性有帮助”（无可争议的事实）“原因如下”，没有任何细微差别（见我对第3.2节的评论）。再次强调，在综述性文章中提出如此强烈的断言而不涉及局限性的细微差别，我认为是有害的。 - 文章结构有时冗余且混乱（例如，6.1.1和6.4.1，详见详细评论） - “开放问题和未来方向”部分的内容不符合描述，因为它 mostly 列举了不符合所提分类的进一步现有工作。我建议重新整理该部分，更好地区分哪些是实际的开放问题和未来方向。 更好的是，一个名为“局限性和未来方向”的部分会更有意义，因为总的来说，所有提出的问题（样本效率、迁移、虚假相关性、可解释性、公平性、安全性）仍然是开放性问题。我还注意到一些关于因果强化学习（causal RL）的相关近期工作在综述中缺失：- Gun等人，ICML 2022，《部分可观测马尔可夫决策过程的可证明高效离线强化学习》- Pace等人，ICML 2023，《非可识别隐藏混淆下的Delphic离线强化学习》- Gasse等人，TMLR 2023，《在潜在模型基础强化学习中使用混淆数据》### 详细评论- 第1页“emerge” -> 打字错误- 第2页：“因果性可以显著提高机器学习模型的鲁棒性和可解释性” -> 我发现整个段落相当模糊且动机不明确。纯粹的“数据驱动”方法、“因果性”和“因果推断”之间的区别并不清楚。在提出的坏血病例子中，经典的在线强化学习算法如REINFORCE或Q-learning可以最优地解决问题，而无需显式地依赖因果性。这里的问题在于手头的数据，实验数据与观察数据。因果性提供了一个框架/一套工具来表达这个问题，但不一定是解决它的方法。基于纯粹的观察数据，因果推断通常是不可行的。我认为这一段在解释问题的本质方面做得非常差，反而误导读者认为因果性是一个通用工具，可以简单地应用于任何机器学习模型，并神奇地提高其鲁棒性。这对于面向领域新人的综述论文尤其成问题。- 第2页“在大多数强化学习研究中，智能体只被允许干预动作变量” -> 这为什么是个问题？出于什么目的这是个问题？强化学习的总体目标是找到一个智能体的最优策略，该智能体只能通过动作变量进行操作。如果最终这些变量不可操作，知道如果可以干预其他变量会发生什么又有什么好处？这里的叙述似乎是“强化学习需要因果性，因为强化学习不能学习因果性”。这里缺失的是，为什么完整的因果模型首先会对强化学习有益？同样，我认为这一段在说明因果性能为现有强化学习算法带来什么方面非常没有说服力且动机不明确。- 第2页“相比之下，在因果强化学习中，你会从分析因果关系到做出明智的假设开始” -> 与之前的评论相同。这个例子具有误导性。传统的（在线）强化学习不需要假设，只要有足够的数据收集，就能导致最优策略。如这里所述的因果强化学习要么需要因果假设，这些假设可能是错误的（迷信、错误信念），要么需要因果知识，而这又需要实验数据来获取。 基于错误假设的因果推理可能是有害的。这是所有因果强化学习方法的一个关键局限，值得成为讨论的一部分。再次强调，我发现这种叙述非常令人困惑，非常片面，并且误导人们相信因果推断总是为强化学习带来益处。- 第3页“因果强化学习的本质、影响和机遇” -> 那局限性呢？- 第4页“definitionn” -> 打字错误 - 第4页“当父集PA(Vi)太小” -> 我不明白为什么小的父集会违反马尔可夫性质 - 第4页“遗漏变量影响V中的多个变量” -> 什么是遗漏变量？它和外生变量一样吗？- 第4页“马尔可夫性质” -> 尚未定义。是哪种马尔可夫性质？- 第4页“潜变量” -> 在你的结构因果模型（SCM）中，潜变量等同于外生变量吗？我觉得在没有澄清的情况下提到外生、遗漏和潜变量是令人困惑的。- 第5页图3a -> 我发现这种概率分布的表示难以阅读。这些饼图如何表示概率分布？- 第5页“水手们会” -> 本来会 - 第8页图4 -> 在部分可观测马尔可夫决策过程（POMDP）设置中，策略无法访问完整状态，不能表示为$do(a \sim \pi(\dot | s_t))$。POMDPs需要不同的策略形式化。作为建议，只呈现更一般的POMDP设置会更简单，并将MDP设置作为特殊情况推导出来（约束条件为$O_t=S_t$）。此外，因果性试图解决的主要问题之一是混杂，这在MDP设置中不会发生。这是聚焦于POMDPs的另一个原因。- 第8页“初始状态可以被视为外生变量” -> 我不认同这种推理。状态、奖励和行动如何能同时是内生变量，而$S_0$是外生变量？在决定初始行动$A_0$时，$S_0$是观测到的还是未观测到的？这是MDP设置还是POMDP设置？- 第9页“同策略强化学习直接从干预数据中学习行动对结果的因果效应。” -> 那么同策略强化学习已经是一种因果强化学习方法了吗？因果性只在离线设置中有用吗？- 第9页“幸运的是 [...] 我们可以通过某些因果推理技术识别出所需的因果效应” -> 这并不总是正确的（可识别性问题）。这句话具有误导性。- 第10页“为什么因果性有助于提高样本效率” -> 论文的标题暗示这是一篇综述文章，但这一部分听起来更像是一篇观点文章。总体语气是“因果性无疑提高了样本效率，原因如下”。这是一个强烈的声明，我认为在没有适当谨慎的情况下提出是有问题的。我理解这一部分表达的观点，但我觉得将其作为普遍真理呈现是有问题的。 因果方法在样本效率以及一般强化学习中的实用性，在理论和实践中的一般设置中仍有待证明。我强烈建议改变这一部分的语气，并增加更多的细微差别，例如：“因果关系如何提高样本效率？”——第10页“因果关系有助于降低复杂性”——这是某一类方法的动机，而非普遍真理。应当如此呈现。“大多数/许多因果强化学习方法受这样一种想法的驱动，即利用问题的真实因果结构将降低学习的复杂性，从而提高样本效率”——第10页“非因果方法通常比因果强化学习方法表现出更低的效率”——同样，这一断言并非普遍真理。我建议采用更谨慎的语气：“在一些受控设置中，非因果方法已被显示比因果强化学习方法表现出更低的效率”，或者“(Seitzer等人，2021)表明，利用因果关系进行探索的方法在机器人操作任务中提高了样本效率”——第10页第3.3节——我喜欢这一节，它对现有工作进行了易懂的总结。然而，小节与第3.2节的讨论高度重复。我建议为了可读性将第3.2节和第3.3节合并，或者直接删除第3.2节。——第22页第6节“超越回报的考量”——我发现这一节的结构令人困惑。6.1.1“利用因果关系提高可解释性”与6.4.1“具有因果关系的可解释强化学习”重复，6.2.2“利用因果关系提高公平性”与6.4.2“具有因果关系的公平强化学习”重复，6.3.2和6.4.3关于安全性的内容也是如此。我建议合并这些部分。——第27页第7节——这一节名为“开放问题与未来方向”，但实际上是现有工作的延续。为何“7.2 具有因果关系的多任务和元强化学习”是一个开放问题，而“4.3.1 适应不同环境”或“4.3.2 适应不同任务”却不是？这种结构在我看来并不合理。——第31页“因果强化学习是一种有前景的方法”——因果强化学习并非单一方法，正如定义2.3所述。

**请求的更改：**
关键：- 重构叙述，特别是引言部分，呈现对因果强化学习更细微的观点，并采用更谨慎的语气 - 修正技术上的模糊和不一致之处 - 更清晰地说明因果强化学习的动机（希望、信念）、目前取得的成就和已证明的内容（成功）、因果强化学习的成本和局限性，以及尚待完成的工作 加强工作：- 改进论文结构 - 在综述中添加缺失的工作

**主张与证据：**
无

**受众：**
是

**反驳意见：**
回复评审人H8ZM：非常感谢您对我们手稿的全面审查和富有洞察力的反馈！ 我们已仔细考虑了您的每一点意见，并进行了必要的修订，具体如下：

> (C2, 3, 4) 提高引言中对因果在强化学习（RL）中作用和局限性的清晰度。为了更好地说明因果RL的动机以及因果与RL的交集，我们用与强化学习更密切相关的现实应用（机器人操控、医疗治疗和自动驾驶）替换了坏血病的例子。我们在第2页新增了图1，并在第1节中加强了对传统强化学习固有局限性的分析（第2页第二段）。在修订稿中，我们还强调了错误假设的后果作为因果RL需要研究的问题之一，并在第7.1节中增加了额外的讨论（第27页第二段）。

> (C7) 小的父母集如何可能违反马尔可夫性质？这里我们引用了Judea Pearl在[1]中第2.2章对马尔可夫假设的讨论：“如果一个模型中的集合$\text{PA}_i$太窄，将存在同时影响多个变量的扰动项，马尔可夫性质将丧失。”也就是说，在这种情况下存在影响多个内生变量的外生变量。因此，当条件为$\mbox{\textbf{PA}}(V_i)$时，$V_i$可能不独立于其非后代变量。

> (C8, 10) 省略变量、外生变量和潜在变量之间的关系。在修订稿中，我们澄清了这三个术语之间的联系（第4页第二段）。省略变量是一个非正式术语，指在此上下文中为抽象而排除在系统外的因素。结构因果模型（SCM）将这些因素称为外生变量，它们影响内生变量的值。如果有外生变量影响多个内生变量，模型将丧失马尔可夫性质。如果我们明确将这些变量作为潜在变量在因果图中表示，可以恢复马尔可夫性质。

> (C9) 马尔可夫性质的界定。在SCM的背景下，这意味着当条件为其父母$\mbox{\textbf{PA}}(V_i)$时，$V_i$独立于其非后代节点。

> (C11, 13) 改进图3a和图4。我们在修订稿中增强了图3a（第5页）的标题，并修改了图4，使其专注于部分可观测马尔可夫决策过程（POMDPs，第8页）。

> (C14) 为什么初始状态可以被视为外生变量？感谢您指出这一点。我们已删除了这一混淆的陈述。

> (C15) 在策略RL是否已经是一种因果RL方法？在策略RL有时可以从干预数据中学习到行动对结果的总效应，但它并不直接构成一种因果RL方法。认为因果RL仅在离线设置中有用的观点也是不正确的。 即使在在线环境中，仍然存在许多需要了解因果关系的问题，例如如何更有效地收集干预数据，如何转移已获得的知识，以及如何分析决策过程中发生的歧视。正如表1-4所示，第3至6节中呈现的大量研究是在在线环境中进行的。（C17, 18, 19）调整样本效率部分的断言语气。我们已经根据您的要求修订了所提到的节标题和文本，以提供一个更细致的视角，包括对局限性的讨论。非常感谢您宝贵的意见！（C20, 21）为清晰起见，合并冗余部分。我们已经根据您的评论合并了相关部分，以提高可读性。（C22）修订第7节以更好地反映内容。在修订后的手稿中，我们已经根据您的建议将第7节的名称改为“局限性和未来方向”，并在第7.1节（第27页）中专门概述了当前方法的局限性。此外，我们明确强调了第3-6节中讨论的问题仍需进一步研究（第26页最后一段）。（C24）关于解决混杂偏倚的额外相关作品。我们已经纳入了您指出的前两篇参考文献（Guo等人，2022年和Pace等人，2023年）的讨论（第16页第三段）。第三篇参考文献（于2023年8月被TMLR接受）是我们已经引用的一篇论文的更新版本。因此，我们已经更新了参考文献以反映这一新版本。（C1, 5, 6, 12, 16, 23）错别字和编辑。感谢您指出这些问题，我们已经根据您的评论进行了修订和检查。再次感谢您宝贵的见解，这对我们工作的改进无疑做出了贡献。[1] Pearl, Judea. _Causality_. Cambridge University Press, 2009.
